case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 13-5-2008 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 4954 of 2003).
full_judgment:
Md Abdul Aziz J: This petition for Leave to Appeal is directed against the judgment and order dated 13-5-2008 passed by a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 4954 of 2003 reversing those dated 25-9-2003 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Brahmanbaria in Title Appeal No. 153 of 2000 reversing the judgment and decree dated 19-9-2000 passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Sarail, Brahmanbaria in Title Suit No. 16 of 1993.

2. Facts, in short, are that respondent Nos. 1 and 2 as plaintiffs brought Title Suit No. 211 of 1981 for declaration that the alleged deed of gift is illegal, void and has been made upon false personation only to deprive the plaintiffs of their lawful properties and, as such, the defendant Nos. 1-4 be directed to evict from the suit property. Plaintiff's case is that property measuring 0.26 acres of land comprised in Plot Nos. 240 and 160 under CS Khatian No. 166 and Hal Mutation Khatian No. 77/4 within Mouza-Morail within Police Station and District-Brahmanbaria with one old building and also 0.51 acres of land comprised in Plot No. 151 within same Khatian, being a pond, total measuring 0.31 acres of land were originally owned and possessed by one Srimati Bimala Banik and her five sons who took Taka 925 as loan from one Kailash Chandra Banik and secured the said loan by mortgaging her property including the suit property and also executed a registered Tamsuk in favour of said Kailash Chandra Banik. Plaintiffs further stated in the plaint that Kailash Chandra Banik was the Korta of the Hindu joint family of the 3 brothers namely, Kailash Chandra Banik, Nabin Chandra Banik and Gobinda Chandra Banik all sons of Ram Kumar Banik. Kailash Chandra Banik being the Korta of the joint Hindu family made the loan to said Bimala Banik and others from the fund of joint property. Thereafter, Kailash Chandra died leaving behind his only son Nabaddip Chandra Banik and his brothers. In the meantime, the aforesaid loanee Bimala Banik failed to pay the loan along with interest for which Nabin Chandra Banik instituted Title Suit No. 506 of 1917 in the 3rd Court of Subordinate Judge, Comilla, which was ultimately decreed on 25-11-1918 AD in favour of the plaintiff Nabaddip Chandra Banik. Plaintiffs' further case is that Sree Nabaddip Chandra Banik purchased the entire mortgaged property and the sale certificate was issued in his favour on 20-7-1920 and the sale was duly confirmed by the executing Court. Thereafter, the plaintiff/auction purchaser Nabaddip Chandra Banik was put to possession of the entire auction sold property including the suit property and the same was being possessed as joint Hindu family property. In the meantime, Nabin Chandra Banik died leaving behind wife Muktamayee, who died later, left two in the family namely the other brother Gobinda Chandra Banik and the son of Kai lash Chandra Banik (aforesaid Nabaddip Chandra Banik). At this stage, the plaintiff asserts that there was amicable settlement of the entire joint property of the said family in between the Survivor Gobinda Chandra Banik and heirs of Kailash Chandra Banik namely Nabaddip Chandra Banik in the year 1959 upon which Gobinda Chandra Banik got the Saham of the suit property and the said Nabaddip Chandra Banik got the Saham of landed property situated at Bazarghat in the District of Agartala, India since the said Nabaddip Chandra Banik left the then East Pakistan and migrated to Bazarghat for ever and never returned back to this part of the Country. The plaintiff further asserts that pursuant to the said amicable settlement the said Gobinda Chandra Banik while possessing his Saham property, sold some portion of the property to others and thereafter during the RS operation the name of said Gobinda Banik son of Ram Kumar Banik was correctly recorded in RS Khatian being No. 83 who thereafter paid rent and taxes in his own name. The aforesaid Gobinda Chandra Banik had three sons namely, the plaintiffs Naresh Chandra Banik, Dharesh Chandra Banik and father of the defendant Nos. 1-4 namely Paresh Chandra Banik. Out of them Paresh Chandra Banik was living in the joint family with his four sons namely, Provash Chandra Banik, Suvash Chandra Banik, Chandan Chandra Banik and Khokan Chandra Banik, who are the defendants Nos. 1-4 of the instant suit. Later the said Paresh Chandra died during the life time of his father Gobinda Chandra Banik. In the year 1970 Gobinda Chandra Banik at his old age executed a deed of gift in favour of plaintiff Nos. 1 and 2, who are his living sons, being registered deed of gift No. 4802 dated 5-6-1970, through which he gifted away all his properties to the plaintiff Nos. 1 and 2 and handed over possession of the same to them including the residential house, on the ground that the defendant Nos. 1-4 are arrogant and regularly making trouble to the plaintiff Nos. 1 and 2. Thereafter, the plaintiff Nos. 1 and 2 mutated their names through Miscellaneous Case No. 493 of 1979-80 and obtained separated mutation khatian No. 77/4 in respect of suit Plot Nos. 160 and 161 in their names along with other properties and paid rent and taxes. Plaintiffs further assert that the defendant Nos. 1-4 being in permissible possession of the suit property under them refused to vacate the property on demand, on the ground that they have obtained registered deed of gift from Nabaddip Chandra Banik on 1-11-1978 and, as such, they are the rightful possessor and title holder of the suit property. Plaintiffs assert that the said deed of gift is a forgery and obtained by false personating only to deprive the plaintiffs of their lawful properties and the defendant Nos. 1-4 are liable to be evicted from the suit property. Hence they instituted the instant suit.

3. The defendant No. 1 Sree Provash Chandra Banik contested the suit by filing written statement, contending, interline„ that complicated question of law related to title and possession in respect of the suit property having been involved in the suit, absence of any prayer regarding either declaration of title or establishment of the same, made the suit non maintainable. The defendant No. 1 further asserts that the family of the three brothers Kailash Chandra Banik, Nabaddip Chandra Banik and Gobinda Chandra Banik was not a joint Hindu family and, as such, Kailash was not the Karta of the said family, rather Kailash from his own fund gave loan of Taka 925 to Bimala Banik and to her five sons upon obtaining mortgage of the property, owned by the said loaner, including the suit property for which after the death of said Kailash, when the loanee failed to pay back the loan amount, the aforesaid Nabaddip for his own interest instituted mortgage Title Suit No. 506 of 1917 and obtained the decree in the said suit, put the same in execution by way of auction and purchased the suit property on public auction through the Court and obtained the sale certificate and delivery of possession which was duly conformed by the executing Court. Thereafter, while Nabaddip Chandra Banik owning and possessing the suit property executed a deed of gift in favour of the defendant Nos. 1-4 on 1-11-1978 through which the defendant Nos. 1-4 obtained right, title and possession in 0.26 acres of land with 50% of the residential building and also 0.05 acres of land in the pond. Thereafter, Nabaddip died leaving behind his four sons, the defendant Nos. 5-8 namely, Sankar, Sukumar, Samorendra and Sattyendra Chandra Banik. The defendant No. 1 asserts that although the plaintiff sold some portion of the property under the suit khatian to strangers but none of them got any right, title or possession in the suit property as the plaintiffs had no right, title and possession in the suit property. The plaintiffs being the first paternal uncle of the defendant Nos. 1-4 residing in a portion of the residential house within the suit property under permissive possession of the defendant Nos. 1-4 and the defendant No. 1 has been in exclusive possession in 0.34 acres of land covered by the deed of gift with entire 50% building thereon and 0.05 acres of land in the tank and he is possessing four rooms of the residential building on the western part and the plaintiffs are in a permissive possession under the defendant No. 1 in two rooms in the eastern portion of the building and two houses of two CI sheet. The defendant No. 1 prayed for dismissal of the suit.

4. Trial Court on 23-5-1991 fixed the suit for hearing but on 26-6-1991 the same was heard and decreed exporter in default of the defendant No. 1 to appear before the Trial Court. Against the ex-parte decree, the defendant No. 1 preferred Title Appeal No. 38 of 1991 before the learned District Judge, Brahman aria, who allowed the appeal and sent the case back on remand to the trial Court for hearing afresh. Subsequently, the said suit was transferred to the Court of Senior Assistant Judge and was renumbered as Title Suit No. 16 of 1993. Thereafter, the learned Senior Assistant Judge upon examination of PWs and DWs and material on record vide judgment and decree dated 14-7-1993 decreed the suit. Against the judgment and decree of the trial Court, defendant No. 1 preferred Title Appeal No. 99 of 1993 before the learned District Judge, Brahmanaria. The suit was again sent back on remand in the trial Court for hearing with certain observation. The trial Court had taken evidence afresh and decreed the suit upon resettling the fresh issue on 19-9-2002. The defendant No. 1 preferred Title Appeal No. 153 of 2003 before the learned District Judge, Brahmanaria against the judgment and decree dated 19-9-2002. The same was heard on transfer by the learned Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Brahmanaria, who vide judgment and decree dated 25-9-2003 allowed the same.

5. Being aggrieved by and dismissed with the judgment and decree of the appellate Court, the plaintiff-opposite-party Nos. 1 and 2 prefer-red Civil Revision No. 4954 of 2003 before the High Court Division and obtained Rule. The learned Single Judge of the High Court Division upon hearing the parties vide judgment and order dated 13-5-2008 made the Rule absolute and set aside the judgment and decree of the appellate Court. Hence this leave petition by the petitioner.

6. M AB Roy Chowdhury, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner, submits, that the appellate Court considered independently the relevant points for adjudication and discussed the evidence led by the parties as well as the point of law and the judgment and decree of the appellate Court did not suffer from patent illegally and material irregularly nor was violative of the provision of Order 41 Rule 31 of the Code of Civil Procedure but the provisional erroneously decided that the appellate Court failed to consider the evidence on record in reversing the finding of the trial Court. He submits that Nabaddip brought Mortgage Title Suit No. 506 of 1917 and obtained judgment and decree and subsequently he purchased the suit land in his own name through public auction for his personal interest but not in the interest of the joint family, but the plaintiffs brought the suit claiming that the entire suit property along with other properties purchased under the auction by Nabaddip in his own name is a property of the whole family of Khalish Chandra Banik and his two brothers without seeking that the suit property was purchased in the name of Nabaddip as being a demander of the suit property, as such the suit of the plaintiffs is not maintainable under Section 42 of the Specific Relief Act but the provisional Court erroneously found that the suit is maintainable without seeking declaration of title under Section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. He submits that the appellate Court perfectly justified in finding that plaintiff did not mention the date and year of the mortgage in question of joint family showing the three brothers as a members of joint family property which is inherited from the father of the Korta of the said family. Moreover, the plaintiff could not prove by producing the CS record of the suit property that the father of the three brothers was the owner of the suit property which was not considered by the Revisional Court. He also submits that upon averments of the plaint Nabaddip was the son of Kailash Chandra Banik but it said Nabaddip was not the Karta of the said joint family but he purchased the suit property through Court in his own name for his personal interest by his personal fund, as such the provisional Court cannot decide that the property has been purchased in the interest of the joint family.

7. We have heard the learned Advocate for the petitioner and perused the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division and other materials available on record.

<u>8. The learned Single Judge of the High Court Division on consideration of the facts and evidence of the case came to the finding that the suit is maintainable in its present form and also found that the suit property was a part of the joint property of the Hindu joint family which has correctly came to the hand of Gobinda Banik through amicable settlement. The learned Single Judge also observed that e-mail property situated in any part of the world may be brought in the hotchpots of the suit according to Section 2 of the Partition Act, 1898. As regards the claim of gift of the defendants of the suit land, the High Court Division found that the defendant Nos. 1 and 4 failed to discharge the onus of proving the deed of their gift dated 1-11-1978 and, as such, the gift was not proved and it observed that the appellate Court below did not apply its judicial mind on the facts and circumstances of the case and the evidence on record and passed. the impugned judgment on a slipshod manner on surmise and conjuncture. On the above finding and observation, the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division made the Rule absolute restoring the judgment and decree of the trial Court setting aside the judgment and decree of the Court of appeal below. On our consideration of the aforesaid findings and observations of the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division, we are of the opinion that the learned Judge has not committed any error in passing the impugned judgment nor there is any misreading or non consideration of the evidence and materials on record by the learned Single Judge in making the Rule absolute. Hence we find no substance in the submission of the learned Advocate for the petitioner.</u>

<u>The leave petition is thus dismissed having no merit.</u>

End.

caseno: Civil Petition for leave to Appeal No. 492 of 2007.
lawyer:
Abdul Quayum, Senior Advocate with JN Deb, Advocate instructed by AKM Shahidul Huq, Advocate-on-record—For the Petitioners. 
Aftab Hossain, Advocate-on-Record—For the Respondent Nos. 1-6.

parties:
Jamira Khatun and others ------ Petitioners 
VS.

case_source: (From the judgment and order dated the 8th day of February, 2006 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 3975 of 2001).
full_judgment:
Md Fazlul Karim J: This Petition for leave to Appeal at the instance of the petitioners is directed against the judgment and order dated 8-2-2006 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 3975 of 2001 making the Rule absolute setting aside the judgment and decree dated 17-7-2000 passed by the Additional District Judge and Anti-Smuggling Tribunal, Sylhet in Title Appeal No. 312 of 1999 affirming those dated 19-10-1999 passed by the Senior Assistant Judge, Additional Court, Sadar, Sylhet in Title Suit No. 50 of 1997 dismissing the suit.

<u>2. The short facts of the case are that the plaintiffs instituted Title Suit No. 216 of 1985 in the First Court of Munsif, Sylhet Sadar, Sylhet impleading the respondent No.1 as principal defendant and the other respondents as proforma defendants for a declaration of their right, title and possession jointly with the proforma defendants in the suit land and also for declaration that the judgment passed in Miscellaneous Case No. 132 of 1969 of the same Court is collusive, illegal, inoperative and liable to be set aside. The suit was subsequently transferred to the Additional Court of Senior Assistant Judge, Sylhet Sadar and renumbered as Title Suit No. 50 of 1997. In the plaint the Suit land was described as District-Sylhet, Thana-Sadar, Mouza-Godnorail, Plot No.1859 SA Khatian No. 192713 appertains to Dag Number 116 of Abdul Taluk Number 1102/30 measuring about 14 acres equivalent to 1/2 Kedar and meets and bounded by, in the east the public path and thereafter the residence of the plaintiffs, in the west the residence of defendant No. 1, in the North the passages of the defendant No. 1 and thereafter Samad and others, in the south the kitchen garden (bichrachara) of the plaintiffs and the suit land is the family graveyard of the plaintiffs as well as of the pro-forma defendants.</u>

3. The defendant No. 1 Nazibulla h contested the suit by filing written statement denying the claims of the plaintiffs stating, inter alia, that the suit land along with other lands belonged to Taluk No.1079 Bakor Mohomad and Niskor Benombary (numberless) Taluk Niamat Ali Shah and Liakat Ali Shah and the disputed land was not part of Taluk No. 1102/30 Abdul Talik; that without local investigation the plaintiffs are not entitled to get any relief, that the plaintiffs, the pro-forma defendants or their predecessor have/-had no right title and possession in the suit land, the plaintiffs and the proforma defendants in collusion with each other instituted the suit, that the kabala in the name of the wife Abdul Khalid dated 12th Baishakh 1326 BS as it mentioned in the plaint do not attract the suit land. Moreover, since the plaintiffs and the proforma defendants had got no right, title and possession over the suit land and the suit is not at all maintainable in its present form inasmuch as the suit land belonged to Abdul Monaf in his Maliki right under his khas possession and while the said Abdul Manaf owned and possessed the land in Maliki right by executing a kabaliyat dated 4-4-1948 they took settlement of 3 kadar 3 powa land from the said Abdul Monaf with a rent of Taka 16 per year and thereafter by taking possession of the suit land has been enjoyment and possessing the same by using it as his family graveyard, as well as in some part of the suit land he has been growing bamboos and trees; that his son, one daughter and one nephew were buried in the said graveyard, but the plaintiffs or their predecessor did never possess the suit land; that though he has been possessing the suit land in the last settlement survey it was recorded in the name of his landlord Abdul Monaf and as such for correction of record he filed Miscellaneous Case No. 139 off 1969 in the First Court of Munsif, Sylhet Sadar under Section 143 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act which was decreed in his favour and accordingly the record was corrected and the judgment passed in that suit cannot be declared or set aside since the plaintiffs were aware of the judgment of the case dated 5-8-1970, moreover, the suit is barred by limitation; that subsequently by two amendment petitions the said Nazibullah amended his written statement twice, by the first amendment the quantum of his alleged settlement with him by Abdul Monaf was increased upto 4 kedar 2 powa, and by the second one the statement regarding burial of the family members of the plaintiff with his permission in the suit land had been struck off. After hearing, the Assistant Judge by his judgment and decree dated 19-10-1999 dismissed the suit with the finding that the suit though is maintainable but barred by limitation with the finding that the suit land belonging to Abdul Taluk as reported by the Advocate Commissioner's report is not reliable, and the defendant has been enjoying and possessing the suit land. On appeal the said judgment was affirmed by the appellate Court by the impugned judgment and decree dated 17-7-2000 agreeing with the findings of the Trial Court.

4. Mr. Abdul Quayum, learned Counsel, appearing for the petitioners submits that the High Court Division while making the Rule absolute did not reverse all the findings and decisions of the Court below; that though the plaintiffs claimed the suit land measuring 0.14 acres as land of 1102/30 Abdul Taluk; but the PW 1 (plaintiff No. 2) who deposed for all the plaintiffs admitted in chief examination that "নাঃ সম্পতি এই তিন পোয়া আমাদেও পূর্ববর্তী আং করিম এর স্বত্ব দখলীয় ছিল" and also in cross examination admitted that "আমরা আব্দুল তালুকের ২২ শং সম্পতি পাব" and he contesting defendant filed the khatian No. 424/5 of Dag No. 1860 (Exhibit-Ga) in the name of plaintiffs for an area of 0.22 acres of Abdul Taluk, All of which clearly proved that the plaintiffs have no right, title and interest over the suit land; that the trial Court while considering the local investigation report specifically stated that without finding or placing a fixed point by the Commissioner the whole work became unwise and accordingly ignored the report as not reliable and also considers the suit Khatian in the name of the defendant as belonging to Baker Mahamud Taluk and Khatian No. 424/5 (Exhibit-Ga) in the name of the plaintiffs as belonging to Abdul Taluk and asserted that the plaintiffs did not raise any question regarding the entries in the Khatian and as such, held the suit land as belonging to Baker Mahmud Taluk that in the suit graveyard there is no burials of any relation of the plaintiffs, rather on the other hand, the brother of the defendant No.1 and son, daughter and a nephew of defendant No. 1 also buried in the suit graveyard which has not been denied by the plaintiffs by cross examining the said defendant No. 1, rather the PW 1 in his cross examination admitted that neither his parents nor his relations were buried in the suit graveyard; that the defendant No.1 on mutating his name in view of judgment and decree as passed in Miscellaneous Case No. 132 of 1969 of the First Court of Sadar, Munsif, Sylhet has been paying rent but on the other hand the plaintiffs are not paying any rent concerning Dag No. 1859 which clearly proves the possession of the defendant No. 1; that the suit is bad for defect of party in view of the fact of non-impleading the heirs of Abdul Monaf in whose name the record of rights were prepared and subsequently corrected by the defendant No. 1 vide judgment and decree dated 5-8-1970 as passed in Miscellaneous Case No. 132 of 1969 and in case of setting aside of the said decree as passed in Miscellaneous Case No. 1 132 of 1969 the record of rights would stand in the name of Abdul Monaf and a decree for declaration of title cannot be given without impleading the heirs of Abdul Monaf as defendant; that the judgment and decree in Miscellaneous Case No. 132 of 1969 was passed on 5-8-1970 and the plaintiffs brought the suit on 19-9-1985 and stated that the plaintiffs came to know about the wrong record of rights in the first part of Srabon 1392 BS; but, could not prove the date by any witnesses and as such, the present suit was hopelessly barred by limitation; that all the 3 PW's are related with each other and in view of the fact and circumstances of the case in absence of any neutral witnesses the plaintiffs cannot get the relief; that the plaintiffs suit as framed is not maintainable inasmuch as the plaintiffs claimed declaration of title for themselves along with pro-forma defendant Nos. 2-9 which is not permissible in law; that there was a suit being Title Suit No. 293 of 1965 in which there was local investigation covering the present suit land and the report dated 5-11-1969 has been filed by the defendant No. 1 in the present suit and the same was marked as Exhibit-'kha' and in that report the suit land has been held as land of Baker Mahamud Taluk and the land of the defendant No. 1

5. It appears from the record that admittedly the suit land is graveyard and the contesting defendant admitted that some family members of the plaintiffs were buried in that graveyard. It appears that in the suit the pertinent question is that the suit land relates to which Taluk. It appears from the report of an advocate commissioner that the suit land belonged to Abdul Taluk as is claimed by the plaintiffs. But the said report was not properly considered by the trial Court with the plea that the investigation was not started from any fixed point, but in arriving into such decision the learned Judge has considered his earlier order of the Court whereby the report was accepted by the order No. 41 dated 02-08-1989 passed by the Assistant Judge and admittedly against that order the defendant moved the Court but was unsuccessful. It appears that the trial Court considered the commissioner's report with a negative approach and the appellate Court do not at all bother to see that report. That in respect of the question of limitation, the High Court Division held that previously there was no cause of action for the plaintiffs to file any suit since they were not disturbed by anybody and the decision of the Miscellaneous Case No 132 of 1969 was not binding upon them since they were not a party in that case.

<u>6. It is apparent that the defendant did not take settlement of any land relating to the Taluk named as Abdul Taluk, rather he may have taken settlement of land relating to other Taluk which is adjacent to the land of Abdul Taluk. Therefore the claim of the defendant has not been established and the Courts below without properly appreciating of that exhibit illegally decided the fate of the suit. It appears that the so-called record of right in the name of Abdul Monaf and subsequently corrected in the name of the contesting defendant by filing a suit under section 143 A of the state Acquisition and Tenancy Act is not at all relevant to the suit land and the plaintiff is not bound by the decree of the suit.</u>

<u>7. The High Court Division as well found that the defendant No. 1 has got no basis of his claim in the suit land, rather, he made the false claim on the basis of an alleged kabuliyat which was not supported by any other document and in support of his such document he could not file any scrap of paper, that after 1951 the so-called kabuliyat, if any, has got no value in the eye of law. The High Court Division observed that the said alleged settlement was not in respect of the suit land. It appears from the rent receipts exhibit-2 series submitted by the plaintiffs that these rent receipts are evidence of possession of the plaintiffs, moreover the contesting defendant himself admitted that some members of the plaintiff family were buried in the graveyard with his permission though subsequently he struck off such admission made in the written statement itself. It appears that the right of adverse possession cannot stand since the defendant claims that he took settlement of the land from his landlord but on his failure to prove his such claim he cannot raise the alternative plea.</u>

<u>8. The High Court Division held that on misreading of evidence and on non-consideration of the evidences on record the Courts below found that the defendant has been enjoying and possessing the suit land, this sort of finding is nothing but illegal occasioning failure of justice. On the contrary, the plaintiffs have been able to prove their right, title and possession over the suit land.</u>

9. In view of the above, we find no substance in the submissions of the learned Advocate for the petitioner.

10. Accordingly, the petition is dismissed.

End.

case_source: (From the judgment and order dated the 8th day of November, 1998 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 1697 of 1994).
full_judgment:
Md Fazlul Karim J: The appeal by leave is directed against the judgment and order dated the 8th day of November, 1998 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 1697 of 1994 discharging the Rule affirming those dated 27-2-1994 passed by the Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Sylhet in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 38 of 1990 allowing the appeal granting temporary injunction reversing those dated 8-3-1990 passed by the Senior Assistant Judge, Sadar, Sylhet in Title Suit No. 241 of 1989 refusing plaintiff's prayer for temporary injunction.

2. The facts involved in this case, in short, are that the plaintiff, Abdul Matalib, was in possession of the suit land by constructing homestead and residing therein with his family for the last 51/52 years on the basis of his jote right and by adverse possession. The defendant No. 4 recently disclosed that Ishaque Ali, predecessor of defendant Nos. 1 and 2 instituted Title Suit No. 34 of 1962 against defendant Nos. 4 and 5 and predecessor of defendant Nos. 6-10 for declaration of title to the suit land and recovery at khas possession of the land and obtained a decree in respect of the suit land. The predecessor of the defendant No. 1 put the decree of Title Suit No. 34 of 1962 into execution in Title Execution Case No. 68 of 1964 and tried to evict the defendant Nos. 4-10 and the plaintiff therefrom. That immediate after filing of the suit, the plaintiff filed an application under Order XXXIX, rule 1 of Code of Civil Procedure for temporary injunction restraining the defendant Nos. 1-3 from evicting the plaintiff from the suit land by putting the decree of Title Suit No. 34 of 1962 into execution.

3. The defendant Nos. 1-2 contested the suit filing written statement contending, inter alia, that they instituted Title Suit No. 34 of 1962 for declaration of title and for recovery of khas possession and that suit was decreed. The defendants in Title Suit No. 34 of 1962 preferred Title Appeal No. 26 of 1964 against the judgment and decree of the Title Suit No. 34 of 1962 which was dismissed. The Title Execution Case No. 68 of 1964 instituted by Ishaque Ali, predecessor of the defendants, was still pending. Ishaque Ali, decree-holder of Title Suit No. 34 of 1962 died on 21-2-1988 leaving his heirs. Osman Ali and Goleza Khatun sold their interest of the land of schedule II of the plaint of defendant No. 2 by a registered kabala dated 9-11-1988 and in this way defendant Nos. 1 and 2 were in possession of the land of schedule II of the plaint. The defendant No. 2 purchased the land of 4 dags out of schedule I of the plaint from one Jamini Kumar Nath and Baikunta Nath by kabala dated 1-8-1969 who were tenants of the landlords Jago Chandra and others. The plaintiffs have no title and possession of the suit land and, as such, the prayer for temporary injunction should be rejected.

<u>4. Leave was granted to consider that submissions of the learned Counsel for the appellants that "the judgment-debtors created series of obstructions when they were unsuccessful and set up the present plaintiff, Abdul Matalib to bring the instant Title Suit No. 241 of 1989 to defeat the execution proceeding and to defeat the decree. The High Court Division failed to comprehend the above aspect and thereby erred in law discharging the Rule. It is the fact that two local investigations in respect of the suit land were held that had the plaintiff been found not in possession, the reports would reveal that fact, and in absence of such report and filing of the instant suit the High Court Division should have come to the conclusion that the plaintiff was a set up person of the judgment-debtors of Title Suit No. 68 of 1962. It was further submitted that the plaintiff had brought the suit at the fag end of the execution proceeding of Title Execution Case No. 68 of 1964 when the decree-holders were going to get the benefit of the decree obtained by their predecessor 30 years back. The plaintiff Abdul Matalib who was not a judgment-debtor did not file any application before the executing Court under Order XXI, rule 90 of the Code of Civil Procedure claiming to be in possession of the suit property."</u>

5. Mr. AJ Mohammad Ali, learned Counsel, appearing for the appellants submitted that the judgment-debtors creating a series of obstruction when became unsuccessful being set up the present plaintiff, Abdul Matalib was set up to file the instant Title Suit No. 241 of 1989 to defeat the execution proceeding and to defeat the decree; that local investigations in respect of the suit land were held on two occasions and had plaintiff been in possession, the reports would reveal that fact and in absence of such report and filing of the instant suit the High Court Division should have come to the conclusion that the plaintiff is a set-up persons of the judgment-debtors of the Suit No. 64 of 1962. The learned Counsel further submitted that the trial Court found that the plaintiff failed to prove prima facie case and possession of the suit land and thereby rejected the prayer for temporary injunction. The learned Counsel finally submitted that the plaintiff has brought the suit at fag end of the execution proceeding of Title Execution Case No. 68 of 1964 when the decree-holders were going to get the benefit of the decree obtained by their predecessors 30 years ago. The plaintiff, Abdul Matalib is not a judgment-debtor, he did not file any application before the executing Court under Order XXI, rule 99 of the Code of Civil Procedure claiming in good faith to be in possession of the suit property on his own account and, as such, the plaintiff has no locus standi to institute the present suit to establish the right which he claims to the present possession of the property, the High Court Division erred in discharging the Rule on the mistaken premises that the plaintiff is in possession of the suit land and thus, entitled to get an order of temporary injunction.

6. Mr. Khurshid Alam Khan, learned Advocate, appearing for the respondent, submitted that the Subordinate Judge has allowed the appeal reversing the judgment and order of the Assistant Judge as the plaintiff proved his prima facie title and possession over the suit land, as such, the High Court Division has not erred in affirming the judgment and order of the Subordinate Judge; that the Subordinate Judge did not commit any illegality in allowing the appeal after setting aside the judgment and order of the Assistant Judge and, as such, the High Court Division has not erred in discharging the Rule and thereby affirming the judgment and order of the Subordinate Judge; that the plaintiff has won both in Court of Appeal below and in the High Court Division, but the Appellate Division has granted leave in order to ascertain whether the High Court Division has rightly discharged the Rule and hence this Civil Appeal arises and the added respondent No. 23 will get all the benefits of the plaintiff-respondent Abdul Matalib and others. The learned Advocate further submitted that the plaintiff has been living in the said dwelling house and enjoying the other land by growing trees, bamboos and using the water of the pond and rearing fish in the pond within the knowledge of all including the defendants. The added respondent No. 23 will get all the benefits of the plaintiff. The learned Advocate finally submitted that the Subordinate Judge in reversing the judgment of the Assistant Judge found possession of the plaintiff over the suit land in view of the report of Nazir, who returned the writ of delivery of possession of Title Execution Case No. 68 of 1964 stating that the plaintiff is in possession of the suit land. The Assistant Judge as it appears did not consider this fact of possession of the plaintiff over the suit land and rejected the plaintiffs prayer for temporary injunction holding that the plaintiff has filed this suit after 27 years of the decree of Title Suit No. 34 of 1962 only to delay execution of the decree and, as such, the Court of Appeal below has rightly set aside the judgment and of the trial Court and the High Court Division has committed no error of law in affirming the judgment of the Court of Appeal below the benefits of which will rightly be accrued to the added respondent No. 23.

<u>7. It appears that the matter arose out of a suit for declaration of title in the suit land with a prayer for recovery of khas possession being a person who does not claim to be judgment-debtor in the previous suit decreed in favour of the appellant. The present plaintiff has brought the suit at the fag end of the execution proceeding of Title Execution Case No. 68 of 1964 for recovery of possession in order to get benefit of the decree obtained by their predecessor 30 years back. As we have already stated that the plaintiff is not judgment-debtor and he has not filed application before the execution Court under Order XXI, rule 99 of the Code of Civil Procedure claiming in good faith to be in possession of the property on his own accord. In the instant suit i.e. a suit for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession, admittedly the plaintiff is out of possession and the order of injunction is designed to obstruct the execution of decree, the subject matter of Execution Case No. 68 of 1964 arising out of Title Suit No. 64 of 1962. The provision of Order XXI, rule 99 is of no assistance to the plaintiff as well as the present suit is not pending against both the parties to the previous suit so as to attract the said provision but the instant application for temporary injunction is simply designed to obstruct the execution of decree obtained 30 years back by the defendant in the instant suit for declaration of title and recovery of possession at the instance of the present plaintiff.</u>

<u>8. Accordingly, the impugned judgment affirming those of Court of Appeal below is hereby set aside and the judgment and order of trial Court is liable to be restored and accordingly restored.</u>

<u>Accordingly, the appeal is allowed without any order as to costs.</u>

End.

full_judgment:
This Rule arises out of judgment and decree dated 14-8-90 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court Khulna in Title Appeal No. 44 of 1988 reversing the judgment and decree dated 13-2-88 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Dumuria, District Khulna in Title Suit No. 493 of 1983.

2. The facts relevant for the disposal of the Rule may briefly be put thus.

3. The petitioner as plaintiff brought Title suit No. 270 of 1981 in the 2nd Court of Munsif at Khulna for declaration of title to the suit land. The suit was subsequently transferred to the court of Assistant Judge Dumuria and renumbered as Title suit No. 493 of 1983. The plaint case is that, the suit land measuring 1.21 acres originally belonged to one Shukchand Mondal who had 8 annas share as recorded in SA khatian No. 48, and 3 annas 4 gandas share in SA Khatian No. 2 of the mouza concerned. Sheikh Chand Mondal died leaving 5 sons namely, Jotin Mondal, Krishna Pada Mondal, Shahittya Mondal, Santosh Kumar Monda land Aditya Kumar Mondal, the defendants Nos. 16-20. While the said defendants were in possession of the land left by their father ''Shuk Chand Mondal, the two sons, defendants Nos. 16 and 17, transferred by registered kabala dated 24-1-74 land measuring .63 decimals of SA Khatian No. 48 and 6 decimal of SA khatian No. 2 to the plaintiff and inducted him into the possession of the land. The defendant No. 18 Shahittya Mondal, another son of Shukhand Mondal, transferred 32 decimal of land comprising SA Khatians Nos. 48 and 20 decimal of land comprising SA Khatian No. 2 by registered kabala dated 30-1-76 to the plaintiff and put the plaintiff in possession of the land. Thus the plaintiff acquired right, title, interest and possession in the land measuring 1.21 acres, and mutated his name in the Revenue Record and has been enjoying the land on payment of rent to the Government. While the plaintiff was in possession of his purchased land the defendant No. 1 filed an application under section 150 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act to review the order of mutation made in favour of the plaintiff in Miscellaneous case No. 40/ 70-80. Having received the notice of the Miscellaneous case the plaintiff came to learn that the defendant Nos. 16 and 17 in collusion with the defendant No. 1 created a kabala dated 10-11-73 in favour of one Samad and Alauddin. On the date of execution and registration of the kabala dated 10-11-73 Shukchand Mondal was alive and he died on 18-12-83. According to the plaintiff, the kabala dated 10-11-73 is a product of fraud and it was made without any consideration and the recipients of the kabala did never enter into possession of the land and the kabala was not acted upon. Further assertion of the plaintiff is that, he came to know that Samad and Alauddin also created another registered kabala on 14-2-75 in favour of one Bhaggyadhar who never entered into possession of the land demised in the Kabala. Defendant No. 1 in collusion with Bhaggyadhor got another kabala registered 15-9-79 by Bhaggyadhar in his favour and the defendant No. 1 also never entered into possession of the land. All these transactions were mere paper truncations. It also transpired subsequently that the defendant Nos. 2-11 obtained some fraudulent and collusive documents which were also not acted upon. The plaintiff further asserted that in Miscellaneous the mutation in favour of the plaintiff was partially cancelled and encouraged by such cancellation the defendants denied the title of the plaintiff in the suit land on 28-8-81 and hence the suit. The plaintiff pleaded that he is a bonafide purchaser for value without knowledge of the transfer by kabala dated 10-11-73 and the subsequent transfer by various kabalas in favour of the defendant No. 1 by amendment petition the exact share of the plaintiff in the khatian was specified and in schedule No. 1 it has been mentioned that the plaintiff''s share in SA Khatian No. 48 is 4 annas and in schedule No. 2 the share of the plaintiff is 17 gandas.

4. The defendant No. 1 contested the suit by filing written statements denying the material allegations as made in the plaint. The defendant''s case is that Shuk Chand died leaving defendant Nos. 16-20 as his heirs, while the said defendants were in possession of the land left by their father the defendant Nos. 16 and 17 sold 1.00 acre of land to Abdus Samad and Alauddin Biswas by registered kabala dated 10-11-73 and the said purchasers entered into possession of 0.64 acres of land and thereafter they transferred the said land to Bhaggyadhar and Ful Chand by registered kabala dated 14-2-75 who in turn sold the land to the defendant No. 1 by registered kabala dated 15-9-79. The defendant Nos. 10-20 sold 9.66 acres of land to one Atul Krishna Mondal by registered kabala dated 4-7-74 and put the purchaser in possession. Subsequently the defendants Nos. 18-20 took back land from Atul Krishna by kabala dated 15-5-78 and thereafter sold that same to the defendant Nos.  2-11 and one Golam Rahman by registered kabala on the same date i.e. on 15-5-78. After the death of Golam Rahman the defendant Nos.  2-11 as his heirs became the owners of the said land. Defendant Nos. 16 and 17 also sold 0.25 acres of land to Golam Rahman on 20-5-78. Thus Golam Rahman acquired 0.66 acres of land in SA khatian No. 48 and 0.25 acres land in SA Khatian No. 2 and the defendant No. 2-11 are in possession of the land and thereafter the defendant Nos. 2-11 sold the said land to the defendant No. 1 by various kabalas. The defendant thus became the owner of the land and he has been in peaceful possession of the land being a co-sharer in both the khatians. Specific claim of the defendant No. 1 is that by purchase as well as by way of inheritance he acquired title and possession in 2.97 acres of land out of 3.29 acres of SA Khatian No. 48 and 2.84 acres out of 4.94 acres of land of SA Khatian No. 2 and accordingly, he has been in possession of the said land and paying rent to the Government. The plaintiff has no manner of possession in the suit land and the documents of title of the plaintiff are fabricated.

5. Parties adduced evidence, both oral and documentary, in support of their respective claims. The learned Assistant Judge upon assessments of the evidence decreed the suit. On appeal preferred by the defendant the decree of the trial Court was set aside. The Appellate Court although found that the plaintiff has right, title and interest in the portion of the suit land but dismissed the suit on the ground that the suit is barred under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. According to the learned Subordinate Judge, the plaintiff ought to have sought relief for partition.

6. Admittedly the suit land belonged to Shuk Chand Mondal, father of the defendant Nos. 16-20. The claim of the plaintiff is that the defendants Nos. 16 and 17 transferred 63 decimal of land comprising khatian No. 48 and 6 decimal of land comprising khatian No. 2 to the plaintiff by registered sale deed dated 24-1-76. The plaintiff''s further claim is that the defendant No. 18 Satya Mondal transferred 22 decimals of land of khatian No. 48 and 20 decimals from khatian No. 2 by deed dated 30-1-76 to the plaintiff. The defendant No. 1 claims that defendants Nos. 16 and 17 transferred 1.00 acre of land to Samad and Alauddin by kabala dated 10-11-73 and the said purchasers got possession upon 64 decimal of land which was transferred to Bhaggyadhar and Fulchand. The plaintiff''s specific allegation in the plaint is that the defendant No. 1 had always been the main man and the mastermind in creating all those kabalas including the kabala dated 10-11-73. The defendant No. 1 is admittedly the nephew of Mondal i.e. his brother''s son. The plaintiffs claim is that the defendants Nos. 16 and 17 had no legal right and legitimate authority to transfer the land of the khatian to Biswas and Alauddin by kabala dated 10-11-73 because Mondal, the father of defendants Nos. 16 and 17, was then alive, and he died on 19-12-73 and this fact was very much know to the defendant No. 1 and also Samad and Alauddin.

7. From the judgment of the trial Court it appears that the trial Court upon assessment of the materials on record found that the suit is maintainable that the plaintiff purchased the suitland in good faith bonafide and he is possessing the land since purchase. The possession of the plaintiff is proved by the corroborative evidence of other PWs. The learned Assistant Judge considering the material statements of DW 1 the contesting defendant, and Ext. 5, the death certificate arrived at a finding that Shukchand died on 19-12-73 and he was alive at the time of transfer made by defendants Nos. 16 and 17 in favour of Abdus Samad and Alauddin by deed dated 10-11-73. The finding of the trial Court is that the defendant possession has not been proved in the suit land. In the above view the trial Judge found that the deeds standing in the name of the defendant so far as it relates to the plaintiff''s land are mere paper transactions, and the plaintiff has been able to prove his title in the suit land.

<u>8. The learned subordinate Judge appears to have misread the evidence, particularly the documentary evidence Ext, 5 the death certificate of Shukchand Mondal and wrongly held that there is no clear and direct proof that Shukchand was alive at the time of sale of the land measuring 1.00 acre by the defendants Nos. 16 and 17 by deed dated 10-11-73. The death certificate having not been denied by the defendant No. 1, nor there is any oral testimony from the side of the defendant that at the time of transfer by defendant Nos. 16 and 17 in favour of Abdus Samad and Alauddin, Shukchand was alive, the finding of the learned Subordinate Judge is held to be perverse not being supported by any evidence. It appears from the judgment of the Appellate Court that the finding of possession arrived at by the trial Court has not been reversed referring to the evidence and therefore the trial Court''s finding that the plaintiffs is in possession is maintained. No reason has been assigned by the learned Subordinate judge, how the title passed toSamad and Alauddin by kabala dated 10-11-73 executed and registered by defendant Nos. 16 and 17 when their father Shukhand Mondal was alive. No valid reason has been assigned how the title of Jatian and Krishnapada was extinguished before their transfer to the plaintiff by deed dated 24-1-76. It is the specific case of the plaintiff that the plaintiff is a bonafide purchaser for consideration without notice of the existence of transfer made by his vendors and to that effect evidence was laid by the plaintiff. The purchase by kabala dated 10-11-73 by Samad and Alauddin, according to the plaintiff, is unauthorised under the provision of law in that the fact that Shukhand was alive was known to both the transferees and the transfer or of the said deed. Apparently there was no contest as to the quantum of land purchased by the plaintiff by the two deeds, but the learned Appellate Judge made out a new case about the proportionate share of the plaintiff in the suit khatian and wrongly held that the trial Court has given more land to the plaintiff than what the plaintiff is entitled to.</u>

9. Next comes the question of maintainability of the suit as per provisions of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. The learned Subordinate Judge having found that there are other co-sharers in the suit khatians who are also possessing the land the plaintiffs must have sought for a relief for partition and thus held that the suit is barred under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act.

<u>10. In order to confront this situation Mr Sk Razzak Ali, the learned advocate has submitted that the learned Appellate Court erroneously held that the suit is barred under the aforesaid provision of law. His contention is the plaintiff being in possession had sought for declaration of his title in the land i.e. the plaintiff is seeking a relief for his entitlement in the suit land which has been denied by the defendant. His further submission is that the plaintiff''s title in respect of his share namely, 4 annas 4 gondas in schedule 1 and 17 gandas in schedule 2 of which he is in possession may be declared and the plaintiff was not able to seek further than a mere declaration of title which he has committed. The possession of the plaintiff has been proved by evidence and that has been found by the trial Court. The finding of possession has not been reversed by the appellate Judge referring to the material evidence. He had further argued that even if it is found that the plaintiff is in joint possession of the land of the suit khatian, still the plaintiff is entitled to a declaration of his title to the extent of his share and in a case like this suit for pure declaration is maintainable. To find support he has placed reliance upon a decision in the case of Joy Narayan Sen Ukil vs Suchitra Debya reported in 1921 Calcutta Law Journal Vol.33 page 502. In the case under reference the plaintiff instituted a declaratory suit, and on the allegation that he was in joint possession of the one third share claimed by him, he did not seek consequential relief. The claim for declaratory relief was resisted on the grounds amongst others that it was barred by limitation and that even it was well founded, in fact, the suit was not maintainable under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act inasmuch as the plaintiff had omitted to claim further relief. The subordinate Judge found on the evidence that the plaintiff was in joint possession of his share and that the claim for declaratory relief was not barred by limitation but the subordinate Judge held, however, that the plaintiff might have claimed further relief by way of partition, and in this view he dismissed the suit. The plaintiff appealed against the decree and has assailed the reason assigned by the Court below for withholding the declaration justified by the facts found. It was held that where the plaintiff is in joint possession of immovable property, whether such possession be actual possession of his share of the whole, or actual possession of a part coupled with constructive possession of the remainder, he is entitled to maintain a suit for declaratory relief with a view to remove a cloud of his title created by the act of the defendant disputing his share. In a suit so framed, declaration of title is all that the plaintiff needs and he is consequently not called upon to ask for consequential relief by way of partition. The proviso to section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, forbids a suit for pure declaration without further relief; but it does not compel a plaintiff to sue for all the relief which could possibly be granted, or debar him from obtaining a relief which he wants unless at the same time he asks for a relief which he does not want. The expression further relief in the proviso to section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, means relief in relation to the legal character or rights as to property which the plaintiff is entitled to and whose title to such character or right the defendant denied is interested in denying; it must also be relief appropriate to and necessarily consequential of the right or title asserted to. It has further been observed that one of the incidents of joint property is that it may be enjoyed jointly, another incident is that a joint character is liable to be terminated. If a co-owner is content to enjoy joint property as such, he should not be driven to seek for partition, merely because his co-owner chooses to dispute the extent of his share. The principle laid down in the case cited is in all fours applicable in the instant case. This view has been consistently followed in various decisions of the courts of the subcontinent including our Courts. When the plaintiff being in possession seeking for declaration he need not seek any further relief as contemplated under the proviso to section 42 of the Specific Relief Act.</u>

11. Mr Abdul Jabbar has appeared for the opposite party and he has contended that the transfer made by the defendant Nos. 16 and 17 on 10-11-73 in favour of Abdus Samad and Alauddin became valid under the principle of feeding the estoppel as contained in section 53 of the Transfer of Property Act, and also in view of the provision of section 115 of the Evidence Act. According to the aforesaid provision of law, the transferees had acquired interest in the land transferred after the death of Shukchand Mondal. The applicability of the principle is to be adjudged in view of the pleading and the evidence of the parties. In the written statements the defendant has not pleaded that the transferors in the deed made erroneous representation at the time of conveying the land to Abdus Samad and Alauddin nor has adduced any evidence to that effect. Nor the defendant has alleged that the defendant Nos. 16 and 17 made declaration as to their interest in the property.

<u>12. The defendant in order to be successful on the scope of the doctrine of estoppel must show that the defendant Nos. 16 and 17 by a declaration, act or omission intentionally caused the predecessor-in-interest of the defendant to believe in certain state of things which they knew to be false and his predecessors acted on such belief but there the defendant failed. But here no case has been made out in the written statements that Jatindra and Krishna Pada Mondal made erroneous representation or declaration or by their act or omission intentionally caused the purchasers in kabala dated 10-11-73 to believe that defendant Nos.  16 and 17 are the real owners of the property. The defendant in view of the facts and circumstances must have the knowledge about the death of Shukchand and the real state of things were known to the parties, so no question of estoppel arises.</u>

13. The principle of section 115 of the Evidence Act has been spelt out in a decision in the case of Radhasyam Cope vs Akterunnessa Begum and others reported in 6 PLR Dhaka page 181. It has said that in order to bring a case within the scope of the doctrine of estoppel the following things are necessary:

1) There must be a representation by a person or his authorized agent to another in any form, a declaration, act or omission.

2) The representation must have been of the existence of a fact and not a future promise or intention which might or might not be enforceable in contract.

3) The representation must have been meant to be relied upon i.e. it must have been made under circumstances which amounted to an intentional causing or permitting belief in another.

4) There must have been belief on the part of that other in its truth.

5) There must have been action of the faith of that declaration, act or omission, that is to say, the declaration, act or omission must have actually caused another to act on the faith of it, and to alter his former position to his prejudice.

6) The misrepresentation or conduct or negligence must have been the proximate cause of leading the other party to act to his prejudice.

14. It was further observed that in order to find an estoppel, the representation, i.e. a party declaration, act or omission must be clear, definite, unambiguous and unequivocal. In the present case considering the pleading of the parties and evidence it appears to me that the real state of things were known to both the parties namely, the transferor and the transferees of the kabala dated 10-11-73, and there is no proof of erroneous misrepresentation and, as such, there is hardly any scope of the operation of section 43 of the Transfer of Property Act.

15. Further contention of Mr Shaikh Ali is that the plaintiff is bonafide purchaser for value without knowledge of prior transfers. This contention need not be considered in view of the observation made above.

16. Mr Abdul Jabbar has contended that the suit land having not been specified and demarcated by boundary the plaintiff is not entitled to any relief in the form of declaration. To substantiate his contention he has cited a decision in the case of Tayebali vs Abdul Khaleque and others reported in 43 DLR (AD) 87. In the case the land was very much specified and demarcated as given in the schedule of the plaint but the possession of the plaintiff or his predecessor donor could not be proved. In the present case the plaintiff is claiming not only the quantum of land as described in the schedule but also the extent of share in the suit khatian and the plaintiff is in possession of his share claimed. In that view of the matter the cited case has no manner of application.

<u>17. Mr Jabbar has further argued that for not having complied with the provision of Order 7 rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure the plaintiff is not entitled to any declaratory decree in respect of an immovable property because the suit land is not specified with boundaries and other particulars. This plea was not taken by the defendant in the written statements nor any issue was framed to that effect nor any case was made out by adducing evidence and further that in this respect it has not been urged before the trial Court and the Appellate Court below that the suit land is unspecified and vague. It is contended for the first time before this Court that the provision of Order 7 rule 3 has not been complied with in claiming the land in the suit. The suit being one for declaration of tithe, no relief has been sought for confirmation of possession or recovery of khas possession. Mr Sk Razzak Ali has contend that in a declaratory decree no execution is necessary. Specification of the land by boundary is required or may be a legal requirement in case of execution of decree for recovery of khas possession or in a decree for confirmation of possession. The plaintiff needs only a declaration as to his entitlement over his share in the land. His contention in this regard appears to be sound and acceptable. but this point was not at all confounded by the plaintiff in the court below. In the 42 DLR''s case (Noor Mohammad Khan and others vs Government of the People''s Republic of Bangladesh and others; page 434) as has been cited by Mr Md Abdul Jabbar, maintainability of the suit was decided on the basis of the plaintiff''s possession and it was held that plaintiff having failed to prove his possession in the suit land simple suit for declaration of his title is barred. So far the specification according to Order 7 rule 3 is concerned the plaintiff has given in the schedule, name of the mouzas, Khatian numbers, plot numbers, the quantum of land as well as the specific share of the plaintiff. Although the boundary has not been given but the plaintiff will be able to manage his possession in his share according to his entitlement in the property. It is not the case that the other co-sharers are claiming that the plaintiff is possessing more land than his share. In view of the above facts and circumstances the provision as laid down under Order 7 rule 3 cannot strictly apply.</u>

18. In view of the above discussion it is held that the learned Subordinate Judge took a wrong view that the suit is barred under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and that the trial Court has given more land to the plaintiff than what he is entitled to and as a result the learned Subordinate Judge has committed error of law occasioning failure of justice. The judgment and decree passed by the learned Subordinate Judge is set aside. The suit is decreed in favour of the plaintiff.

In the above view, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs.

End.

full_judgment:
Bijan Kumar Das J: This petition for leave to appeal is directed against the judgment and order dated 9-9-1993 passed by the Subordinate Judge, Moulvibazar in Miscellaneous Case No. 7 of 1992 directing the appellant-petitioner to deposit half of the decretal dues or in lieu thereof Bank Guarantee by 23-9-1993.

2. The respondent, Pubali Bank Limited, instituted Artha Rin Suit No. 7 of 1991 in the Court of the Artha Rin Adalat, Moulavibazar impleading the present appellant as defendant No. 3 and respondent Nos. 2 and 3 as other defendants praying for a decree for recovery of Taka 16,81,118/10 together with interest © 20% per annum paid as loan and by judgment and decree dated 19-2-1992 the suit was decreed ex parte decreeing the suit for recovery of Taka 16,81,118.10 paisa from the defendant together with interest at the rate of 20% per annum with effect from 12-4-1991 till realisation subject to payment of necessary court fees.

3. The present appellant then filed Miscellaneous Case No. 7 of 1992 under Order IX rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure praying for restoration of the suit upon setting aside the ex parte decree on the ground that the appellant was prevented by sufficient cause from appearing in Court when the suit was called on for ex parte hearing. The trial Court by the impugned order dated 9-9-1993 directed the appellant-petitioner to deposit half of the decretal dues or Bank Guarantee by 23-9-1993.

4. Being aggrieved thereby the petitioner-appellant preferred this appeal before this court on the grounds, amongst others, that direction to deposit half of the decretal amount by the trial Court tantamounts to refusal to set aside the ex parte decree.

5. Mr Md Mahbub Ali, the learned Advocate, appeared for the appellant.

6. Mr Zakir Hussain, the learned Advocate appears on behalf of the respondent No. 1.

<u>7. We have heard the learned Advocates and perused the impugned order and all other connected papers. The suit for recovery of loan money was filed before the Artha Rin Adalat on 21-5-1991 and the suit was decreed ex parte against the defendants on 19-2-1992. The present petitioner who was defendant No. 3, filed Miscellaneous Case No. 7 of 1992 on 1-4-1992 and the impugned order was passed on 9-9-1993. It appears that the impugned order was passed in view of the amendment made in Artha Rin Adalat Ain which came into force on 17-7-1992. By the said amendment, Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure was made available to a judgment debtor on deposit of half of the decretal dues or furnishing Bank Guarantee of the said amount. The trial Court appears to have passed the order on the basis of the amended Artha Rin Adalat Ain overlooking that Miscellaneous Case No. 7 of 1992 was filed prior the amendment came into force. Artha Rin Adalat Ain 1990 provided only one appeal before the High Court Division against the judgment and decree passed ex parte or on contest on deposit of half of the decretal dues furnishing Bank Guarantee. There was no provision for filing a Miscellaneous Case under Order IX rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure in the original Artha Rin Adalat Ain. When the Miscellaneous Case No. 7 of 1992 was filed under Order IX rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure on 1-4-1992 there was no such provision for filing a Miscellaneous Case under Order IX rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The trial Court therefore committed a gross error of law in failing to notice that the Miscellaneous case filed under Order IX rule 13 was not entertainable at the relevant time against an ex parte decree passed by the Artha Rin Adalat in Artha Rin suit for recovery of loan money. Mr Md Mahbub Ali, the learned Advocate for the appellant candidly referred to a decision in the case of MAC Proprietor Mahtabuddin Chowdhury and another vs Agrani Bank Thatari Branch Dhaka reported in 47 DLR 233 where a Division Bench in a similar case took a view that an aggrieved party i.e. a judgment debtor, has only the forum of appeal when a decree is passed either on contest or ex parte. Provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure are applicable subject to this special law. In the said decision a Division Bench considered sub-sections (4) and (5) of section 5 of Artha Rin Adalat Ain and section 7(1) and (2) of the said Ain and held—"This Artha Rin Adalat Ain is a special law under which courts were constituted which has its own forum of appeal. So, by way of interpreting the provisions of sub-sections (4) and (5) of section 5 it cannot be found that this is an ordinary Civil Court for all practical purposes and all the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure are applicable in the proceeding . The provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure are applicable subject to the provisions of this special law. In the said decision a Miscellaneous Case under Order IX rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure was filed before the Artha Rin Adalat which dismissed the said case on the finding that the summons of the suit was duly served. The aforesaid case under Order IX rule 13 arose out of an ex parte decree passed in a title suit for realisation of some money. The Division Bench in the said case ultimately held that Miscellaneous case under Order IX rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure was not available to the judgment debtor at the relevant time. This Division Bench decision completely covers the facts of the present case before us. The judgment and decree passed ex parte on 19-2-1992 could be set aside by filing a Miscellaneous Case under Order IX rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure as Order IX rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure was not available at the relevant time to the judgment debtor. In such facts Miscellaneous Case No. 7 of 1992 filed under Order IX rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure was not entertainable and accordingly, the present appeal is not maintainable</u>

In the result, this appeal is dismissed without any order as to costs.

End.

full_judgment:
Sheikh Abdul Awal J: This revisional application under section 115(4) of the Code of Civil Procedure is directed against the judgment and order dated 4-5-2006 passed by the learned District Judge, Lakshmipur in Civil Revision No. 7 of 2005 affirming the judgment and order dated 25-11-2004 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, Court No. 1, Lakshmipur in Miscellaneous Case No. 38 of 2004 arising out of Artha-Decree Execution Case No. 15 of 2003, pending in the Artha Rin Adalat and Joint District Judge, Court No. 1, Lakshmipur directing the petitioner to deposit 25% of the decretal amount of the Artha Rin Suit No. 1 of 1998 as security.

2. Material facts of the case as necessary for the disposal of the Rule are that the opposite party No. 1 Pubali Bank Ltd as plaintiff instituted Artha Rin Suit No. 1 of 1998 against the opposite party Nos.2-4 as defendants for realization of its outstanding dues amounting to Taka 30,59,521.25 as on 28-1-1998. During the tendency of the suit the present petitioner by filing an application under Order I Rule 10 CPC for addition of party added as defendant No. 4 in the suit.

3. Ultimately, the suit was decreed ex parte by the ex parte judgment and decree dated 17-3-2003. After getting the ex parte decree the decree-holder-Bank in usual course put the decree in execution by filing Artha Execution Case No. 15 of 2003 before the Artha Rin Adalat and Joint District Judge, Court No. 1, Lakshmipur. In the said execution case the petitioner filed an application on 19-5-2004 under Order XXI, rule 58 CPC praying for exclusion of 0.42 acres of land appertaining to plot No. 1222 of Khatian No. 891 under Samsherabad along with structures standing thereon on the ground that on the date of mortgage as well as attachment the judgment-debtor-opposite party Nos.2-4 were not in possession of the said property, the possession of the said property was delivered to the petitioner on 10-10-1994 by the judgment debtor-opposite party No. 3 on receipt of Taka 10(ten) lacs on the basis of a contract and since then the petitioner (defendant No. 4) has been possessing thereon by constructing a building.

4. The said application was registered as Miscellaneous Case No. 58 of 2004. The decree-holder-Bank by filing written objection resisted the same contending, inter alia, that the application is barred by section 32(2) of the Artha Rin Adalat AM, 2003 inasmuch as the petitioner filed the said application as 3rd party claimant without depositing 25% of the decretal amount.

5. The Artha Rin Adalat upon hearing the application was pleased to pass an order of 25-11-2004 directing the petitioner to deposit security money equal to 25% of the decretal amount by 20-1-2005 in default the application shall stand rejected.

6. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid order dated 25-11-2004 the petitioner filed Civil Revision No. 7 of 2005 under section 115(4) of the- Code of Civil Procedure in the Court of District Judge, Lakshmipur.

7. The learned District Judge, Lakshmipur upon hearing the parties and on considering the material on record by his judgment and order dated 4-5-2006 rejected the Revision holding that the petitioner being a 3rd party ought to have deposited 25% of the decretal amount as per express provision of section 32(2) of the AM, 2003. Against which the petitioner moved this Court and obtained the present Rule.

8. Mr Khair Ezaz Maswood, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner after placing the impugned judgment and other materials on record submits that the learned District Judge seriously erred in law in passing the impugned judgment and order without properly applying his judicial mind into the facts and circumstances of the case and law bearing on the subject and the same has resulted in error in the impugned decision occasioning failure of justice. Drawing our attention to the provisions of section 32(2) and 6(5) of the Ain, 2003 Mr. Ezaz Maswood submits that the petitioner is not a 3rd party inasmuch as section 6(5) of the AM, 2003 provides the description of the 3rd party that is mortgagor and 3rd party guarantor' and in this case the petitioner is neither a mortgagor nor a 3rd party guarantor and as such, the impugned judgment and order is liable to be set-aside.

9. On the order hand, Mr Md Mamunur Rashid, the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite party No. 1, Pubali Bank Ltd. supports the impugned judgment and order which was, according to him just, correct and proper. Referring to the provisions of section 32(2) and 6(5) of the Ain, 2003 Mr Mamunur Rashid submits that from a combined reading of those sections it would be clear that the present petitioner is a 3rd party and it has been consistently held by this Court in so many cases that the Artha Rin Adalat AM being the special statue providing to deposit 25% of the decretal amount as a pre-condition for filing an application by the 3rd party claimant is mandatory and as such, the question of interference does not arise at all. Mr Mamunur Rashid finally submits that the grounds taken in the revisional application as well as the contentions as raised by the learned Advocate for the petitioner is totally misconceived and untenable.

10. We have heard the learned Advocates of the both sides, perused the revisional application along with other connected papers as filed therewith. Now, let us look first at the relevant provisions of the Ain, 2003 with regard to prefer an application by any person aggrieved by the decree passed by the Artha Rin Adalat.

11. In order to resolve the dispute the provisions of section 32(1) and (2) of the Ain, 2003 are required to be referred to for having a better view of the dispute in question. Section 32(1) and (2) of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 reads as follows:

(১) অর্থ আদালতের ডিক্রি বা আদেশ হইতে উদ্ভুত জারী মামলায় কোন তৃতীয় পক্ষ দেওয়ানি কার্যবিধি আইনের বিধানমতে দাবী পেশ করিলে, আদালত প্রাথমিক বিবেচনায় উক্ত দাবী সরাসরি খারিজ না করিলে, ডিক্রিদার অনূর্ধ্ব ৩০(ত্রিশ) দিবসের মধ্যে উহার বিরুদ্বে লিখিত আপত্তি দায়ের করিয়া শুনানি দাবী করিতে পারিবেন

(২) উপরোক্ত মতে দাবী পেশ করিবার ক্ষেত্রে দরখাস্তকারী , ডিক্রিকৃত অর্থের ২৫% সংশ্লিষ্ট সমপরিমাণ জামানত দাখিল করিবে অনুরূপ জামানত দাখিল না করিলে দাবী অগাহ্য হইবে।

<u>12. From a plane reading of the above quoted provisions, it manifests that any third party may submit has claim in any execution case arisen out of a decree or an order of the Artha Rin Adalat after making deposit of 25% decretal amount as security otherwise, the Adalat shall reject the claim.</u>

<u>13. Since the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 being a special statute and there is specific provision for submitting any claim of a third party in any execution case arisen out of a decree or an order of the Artha Rin Adalat the Courts below having rightly directed the petitioner to deposit 25% of the decretal amount as security otherwise, the application shall stand rejected and we endorse the reasonings given by the Courts below.</u>

<u>14. Now coming to the 2nd question as raised by Mr Ezaz Maswood that the petitioner can not be treated as a 3rd party as contemplated by section 6(5) of the Ain, 2003. To meet this argument, we have carefully examined the provisions of section 6(5) and other related sections of the Ain, 2003 together with the application under Order XXI rule 58 of the Code of Civil Procedure and it appears to us that the Courts below under the legal obligation rightly treated the claim to the petitioner as 3rd party's claim.</u>

15. In this connection, we asked the learned Advocate for the petitioner to enlighten us as to how the petitioner would not be treated as 3rd party in the facts and circumstances of the case and law bearing on the subject keeping in mind that the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 being a special statute providing special forum for realisation of loan granted by financial institution. Mr Khair Ezaz Maswood has failed to lay his hands on any provision of the Ain, 2003 empowering the Adalat to accept his plea or grievance.

<u>16. On an overall consideration of the facts, circumstances of the case and law bearing on the subject, we are led to hold that both the Courts below having decided the case on consideration of the materials on record and in accordance with law, the same calls for no interference.</u>

17. In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to cost. The order of stay granted earlier by this Court stands vacated.

The Artha Rin Adalat concerned will however expedite the proceeding of the execution case.

Let a copy of this judgment along with lower Court's record be sent down at once.

End.
