full_judgment:
Md. Joynul Abedin J: This appeal by leave is directed against the judgment and order dated 10-6-1998 passed by a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 1568 of 1997 discharging the Rule issued against the judgment and decree of the learned Additional District Judge, Gazipur passed in TA No. 113 of 1992 setting aside the judgment and decree passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, 2nd Court, Gazipur in TS No. 10 of 1992 decreeing the suit.

2. The appellant as plaintiff filed TS No. 78 of 1990 in the Court of the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Gazipur which was subsequently renumbered as TS No. 10 of 1992 in the 2nd Court of the Additional Assistant Judge, Gazipur for declaration that TS No. 308 of 1973 and the ex parte decree obtained therein by the defendant No. 1, Gopal Baroi, is forged, fabricated, collusive, void and not binding upon the plaintiff on the allegations that the suit property comprising 11.55 acres of land as described in the schedule to the plaint originally belonged to the Zaminder of Kashimpur and accordingly, the CS Khatian was prepared in the name of the said Zaminder. The government by virtue of two different notifications dated 15-12-1953 and 31-3-1985 published in the official Gazette vested the suit land in the Forest Department of the Government. Since then, the Forest Department of the Government has been looking after and managing the same. SA and RS Khatian was therefore prepared in the name of the Forest Department. The defendant Nos. 2 and 3, by creating some forged documents of the suit land, filed TS No. 29 of 1984 in the Court of the Assistant Judge, Kaliakoir, Gazipur for declaration of their title therein. The said suit was dismissed on 30-4-1986 on contest but no appeal was preferred against the aforesaid order of dismissal. Defendant Nos. 2 and 3 then with a view to grabbing the suit land created a forged and collusive ex parte decree dated 3-4-1977 in TS No. 308 of 1973 of the court of Munsif, 2nd Court, Dhaka in favour of defendant No. 1, Gopal Baroi. The plaintiff-appellant thereafter having come to know about the said ex parte decree in TS No. 308 of 1973 submitted on 19-3-1990 an information slip to the Sheristadar of the said 2nd Court of Munsif, Dhaka now Gazipur to inform as to whether any suit being TS No. 308 of 1993 was ever filed by the defendant No.1 against the Government. The Sheristadar of the court of Munsif, 2nd Court, Dhaka now Gazipur thereupon informed in writing on 25-3-1990 that no such suit was filed as the relevant suit register did not show filing of such a suit in the court of Munsif, 2nd Court, Dhaka.

3. Defendant Nos. 2-7 contested the suit contending that the suit was not maintainable and it was also barred by limitation. The said defendants claimed that the suit land originally belonged to Zaminder of Kushimpur and the CS record was prepared accordingly, Defendant No. 1, Gopal Baroi, took settlement of the suit land from the said Zaminder and he was in possession of the same on payment of rent. But the SA Khatian was wrongly prepared in the name of the government for which the defendant No. 1 as plaintiff instituted TS No. 308 of 1973 in the court of Munsif, 2nd Court, Dhaka and it was decreed ex parte on 18-8-1974 declaring the title of the defendant No.1 in the suit land. Thereafter, the defendant No. 1 as plaintiff instituted TS No. 29 of 1984 in the Court of Assistant Judge, Kaliakoir, Gazipur for permanent injunction against the government and the suit was dismissed for some defects but the said dismissal did not affect the right, title and interest of the defendants in the suit land. Subsequently, defendant Nos. 2 and 3 purchased a part of the suit land by registered kabala dated 28-12-1983 from the defendant No. 1. Defendant No. 1 also transferred 2.4 acres of land to one Abdul Awal who in his turn transferred the same to defendant No. 7 by registered kabala dated 10-10-1983. Defendant Nos. 2, 3 and 7 are thus in possession of their purchased land after getting their names mutated on payment of rent to the Government. Defendant Nos. 2, 3 and 7 subsequently sold some land to the defendant Nos. 4-6 by a registered kabala. Defendant Nos. 2 and 3 are in possession of their purchased land after constructing a two-storied building in a portion of the suit land and also by cultivation of the remaining land. The plaintiff has no right, title, interest and possession in the suit land and the gazette notification in the name of the Forest Department of the Government is illegal as it was never acted upon and the suit is liable to be dismissed.

4. The learned Assistant Judge after consideration of the evidence and materials on record decreed the suit. Defendant Nos.2 and 3 thereafter preferred TA No. 113 of 1992 and the learned Additional District Judge, Gazipur upon hearing the appeal allowed the same and set aside the judgment and decree of the learned Assistant Judge dismissing the suit on the ground that the suit was not maintainable as framed, as there was no prayer for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession and that the suit was also bad for defect of parties. The learned Additional District Judge while dismissing the suit as above also held that the plaintiff became the owner of the suit land in view of the said gazette notifications, Exts 1 and 1(a) and the same have not yet been set aside or rescinded; but the right, title and interest of the Government over the suit land extinguished because of the mutation of the names of the defendant Nos. 2 and 3 and others on record and receipt of rent from them by the Thana Revenue Officer.

5. The plaintiff-appellant thereafter preferred a revisional application before the High Court Division and the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division discharged the Rule affirming the judgment of the learned Additional District Judge to the extent that the suit, as framed, is not maintainable in the absence of any prayer for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession and also for defect of parties while disapproving the finding that the right, title and interest of the government acquired by virtue of the said notifications were extinguished because of the mutation of the names of the said defendants and receipt of rents from them by the concerned authority in the Government.

6. The leave, thereafter, was granted to consider whether, in the facts and circumstances of the case, the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division acted in accordance with law in dismissing the present suit by discharging the Rule in the aforesaid civil revision on the ground that the suit was not maintainable in the absence of any prayer for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession and the suit was also bad for defect of parties in view of section 99 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

7. In the present case, the plaintiff has asserted in the plaint that the suit land has vested in the Forest Department of the Government as reserved forest in view of the Gazette notifications dated 15-12-1953 and 31-3-1985 and the Forest Department has been in control and possession of the same. It is also asserted by the plaintiff that the defendant Nos. 2 and 3 filed Title Suit No. 29 of 1984 for declaration of title to the suit land and the same was dismissed on contest. But the said defendants did not prefer any appeal against the aforesaid judgment of dismissal and instead sought to claim their right, title and interest in the suit land on the basis of spurious judgment and decree passed in Title Suit No. 308 of 1973 allegedly filed by the defendant No. 1, but, in fact, there was no such suit filed by the defendant No. 1 and no such decree was obtained by him (defendant No. 1) and the said judgment and decree being spurious were not binding on the plaintiff.

8. It is noticed that the aforesaid gazette notifications have not yet been challenged and set aside by any court of law. By virtue of these two notifications the Government in the Ministry of Forest has acquired right, title and interest in the suit land which still subsist. In this view of the matter, the fact of mutation of the names of the defendants and the receipt of rents from them by the Thana Revenue Officer will not extinguish the right, title and interest of the government in the suit land so long the said notifications subsist. This state of affairs is further bolstered and reinforced by the fact that TS No. 29 of 1984 filed by the defendant No. 1 against the government was admittedly dismissed on contest meaning that the possession and the prima facie title in the suit land is with the government. The learned Single Judge, although dismissed the suit by discharging the Rule, held the same view as under:

"The suit land as admitted vests in the Forest Department of the Government of Bangladesh as per Gazette Notifications Exhibits 1 and 1(a) and these notifications have not been cancelled or rescinded and, as such, it cannot be said that the right, title and interest of the Government over the suit land had been extinguished merely because the Thana Revenue Officer, Kaliganj, Gazipur mutated the suit land in the name of the defendant Nos. 2 and 3 and others and realised rent from them."

9. The learned Single Judge of the High Court Division, while concurring with the finding of the trial Court that the plaintiff-appellant succeeded in proving that the judgment and decree passed in Title Suit No. 308 of 1973 were forged and fraudulent, observed that the defendant Nos. 2 and 3 were under legal obligations to prove their case that the said judgment and decree were genuine and valid by calling for and producing the relevant suit register and the record of the said suit but they failed to do so.

<u>10. Against this backdrop, the question that falls for consideration is, whether the learned Single Judge was correct in law in dismissing the present suit for the reason that there was no prayer in the plaint for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession in the suit land and also for defect of party in that the Deputy Commissioner, Gazipur representing the Government was required to be impleaded as the plaintiff in place of the Divisional Forest Officer, Dhaka Division.</u>

<u>11. A suit for declaration is maintainable under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act as to any legal character or to any right as to any property of the plaintiff if the defendant denies or is interested to deny his title to such character or right. If the above conditions are satisfied, the plaintiff need not ask for any further relief than a mere declaration. But such suit would not be competent and maintainable and the court shall not make such declaration if he, being able to seek further relief than mere declaration to the above effect, omits to do so by way of consequential relief. Whether any other prayer by way of consequential relief is required to be made is determined with reference to the scope of the plaint i.e. the allegations made in the plaint, and not with reference to the allegations in the written statement. The case of Siddique vs Bhupendra Narayan, 13 DLR 544 is on the point under consideration.</u>

<u>12. In the present case, the aforesaid gazette notifications have vested the Government in the Ministry of Forest with the right, title and interest in the suit land and with the subsistence of these two notifications the government in the Ministry of Forest still continues to have the right, title and interest in the suit land. Hence, there was no legal requirement for the plaintiff to make a prayer for declaration of title to the suit land. Similarly, since it is asserted in the plaint that the plaintiff has been maintaining its possession and control of the suit land it was also not necessary for the plaintiff to incorporate a prayer in the plaint for recovery of khas possession. In this view of the matter, the learned Single Judge in the High Court Division fell into an error in dismissing the suit as not maintainable on the ground that the plaintiff did not ask for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession of the suit land. Similarly, we also do not agree with the learned Single Judge that the present suit suffers from defect of party for failing to implead the Government as plaintiff instead of the Divisional Forest Officer, Dhaka Division, rendering the suit liable to be dismissed on that account in view of section 99 of the Code of Civil Procedure. This has been a case of mere mis-description of the plaintiff. Such mis-description of the plaintiff can at best be taken to be a technical defect and it should not be allowed to defeat the ends of justice. The policy underlying sections 21 and 99 of the Code of Civil Procedure is that when a case has been decided on merit, it should not be reversed unless it has resulted in failure of justice. Since the present case has been decided on merit, the mere mis-description of the plaintiff shall not be allowed to affect the suit, particularly when the mis-description of the plaintiff in the present suit has not affected the merit of the controversy or the jurisdiction of the court. The present suit, as framed, is found to be maintainable and the judgment and decree dated 29-9-1992 passed by the trial Court is restored.</u>

<u>The appeal, for the above reason, is accordingly, allowed with costs at all stages.</u>

End.

full_judgment:
Sharif Uddin Chaklader J : This rule was issued calling upon the opposite party to show cause as to why the judgment and order No.1 dated 24-4-2005 passed by the learned District Judge, Dhaka in Civil Revision No.406 of 2005 summarily rejecting the petitioner's Civil Revision application under section 115(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 impugning the judgment and order No. 22 dated 14-7-2005 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 4th Court Dhaka in Money Execution Case No. 2 of 2004 rejecting the petitioner's application filed for dismissal of the said Money Execution proceeding and/or such other further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. The short facts relating for disposal of the rule are that, the opposite party obtained decree on 27-3-2000 in Civil Case No.784 of the Federal Court of First Instance, Abu Dhabi City, United Arab Emirates and put the said decree into execution in the Court of Joint District Judge, Dhaka through Money Execution Case No. 2 of 2004. The petitioner filed application for rejection of the Money Execution case as per provisions of Order VII Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The said application was rejected by the learned Joint District judge Dhaka by order No.14 dated 28-11-2004. The petitioner, thereafter, filed another application for the same relief. By the order dated 14-7-2005 the learned Joint District judge rejected the said application. Against which the petitioner moved before the learned District Judge in Civil Revision No. 406 of 2005. The learned District Judge summarily rejected the same on 24-8-2005.

3. Mr Md Mustafizur Rahman Khan, learned Advocate, appearing for the petitioner, submits that, section 44A(i) of the Code of Civil Procedure after amendment in 2003, stand for execution of any decree passed by a Court which has no reciprocating territory of Bangladesh Court as such, decree obtained in such country is unexcitable in Bangladesh. Learned Advocate on referring to the application filed by the petitioner for reconsideration of earlier order before the learned Joint District Judge referred to paragraph 8 of the said application where the petitioner placed before the Court as "according to mandatory provisions and settled principle of law related to Section 44A(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure, the judgment and decree of Abu Dhabi Court, UAE are not executable in Bangladesh in any manner whatsoever in any Court as the UAE is not being or of a Court of a "Reciprocating Territory" and, as such, the present execution case being not maintainable under the said Section 44A(1) of CPC is liable to be rejected with cost."

4. Learned Advocate further submits that, second application filed by the petitioner for the same relief before the learned joint district Judge in not any way stand as bar in the revision before the learned Judge for not paying any relief against the refusal of 1st application and cannot stopped the learned district Judge in giving relief to the petitioner as the decree cannot be executable in Bangladesh as law does not permit so, the Courts below committed gross illegality in not considering the application under Order VII Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

5. The question is very limited as whether UAE is reciprocating territory of Bangladesh and if not, then according so Section 44A of the Code of Civil Procedure whether the decree . can be executable in Bangladesh.

6. Let us fall back on Section 44A of the Code of Civil Procedure, particularly explanation 2 of Section 44A of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 as amended by the Code of Civil Procedure (Third Amendment) Act, 2003 which provides as :—

"Reciprocating territory means any territory as the Government may, from time to time, by notification in the official Gazette, declare to be reciprocal ting territory for the purposes of this Section and 'Superior Courts', with reference to any such territory, means such Courts as may be specified in the said notification."

7. It appears from the judgment of the Courts below that the learned Judges did not consider whether United Arab Emirates in a reciprocating territory of Bangladesh and if so, whether any notification as required under law, was published in the official gazette as per provision of law, (under Section 44A) as notification to that effect is to be published year to year. Bangladesh and India declared to be 'Reciprocating Territory' by simultaneous gazette notification dated 1-7-76 and 1-2-76 respectively. The opposite party decree holder did not produce any paper before the Courts below to that effect as such, we are of the view that the Court below acted illegally in rejecting the application filed by the petitioner.

8. There as other questions involve in this rule which needs to be answered.

9. The foremost question is whether decree holder Janata Bank filed the execution case before the learned Joint District Judge legally. It is an admitted fact the decree holder Janata Bank is a financial institute within the meaning of Section 2 of Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003, Act VII of 2003 and this Ain provides realization of decreetal amount, as such, the execution case, as per provision of law, ought to be filed before Artha Rin Adalat, not before Joint District Judge. It may be, as per sub-Section 4 of the AM, Joint District Judge constitute Artha Rin Adalat, but unless there be a notification through gazette, Joint Districtinnot act as Artha Rin Adalat.

10. Next, the question where the execution case is to be filed, if the question of Artha Rin Adalat push aside and whether it was legally filed. Here we refer to section 44A of the Code of Civil Procedure which runs as:—

"Where a certified copy of a decree of any of the superior Courts of the United Kingdom or any reciprocating territory has been filed in a District Court, the decree may be executed in Bangladesh as if it has been passed by the District Court. "

11. Together with the certified copy of the decree, a certificate shall be filed from such superior Court stating the extend, if any, to which the decree has been satisfied or adjusted and such certificate shall, for the purposes of proceedings under this section, be conclusive proof of the extend of such satisfaction or adjustment.

12. The provisions of section 47 shall as from filing of the certified copy of the decree apply to the proceedings of a District Court executing a decree under this section, and (deemed to be excluded as section 47 has been omitted by amendment) the District Court shall refuse execution of any such decree, if it is shown to the satisfaction of the Court that the decree falls within any of the exceptions specified in clauses (a) to (f) of section 13"

13. District Court mentioned means only the Court of District Judge and certified copy of the decree shall be filed in the Court of District Judge for its execution, not to Joint District Judge. There is a difference between District Court and District Judge. District Court means the principal civil Court of a district and District Judge means the Judge of a principal civil Court, not to any one inferior. When execution of a foreign decree is required, if must filed before the District Judge, no to any other Judge. Here, we may refer to the decision of Sonali Bank vs Abidur Rahman wherein it is held as—

"'The District Court' mentioned in Section 44A(I) of the Code means only the Court of District Judge. In other words, the certified copy of decree under Section 44A(I) of the Code must be filed in the Court of District Judge."

<u>14. From all the discussions made herein above we are of the view that the Courts below totally misread the provisions of section 44A of the Code of Civil Procedure and thereby arrived at a totally illegal findings in holding that the execution case was filed legally before the Joint District Judge and rejected the application filed under Order VII Rule 11 of the Code. We find substance in the rule.</u>

15. In the result, the rule is made absolute without any order as to cost. The Money Execution Case No.2 of 2004 pending in the Court of learned Joint District Judge, Dhaka is dismissed.

16. Before parting writ the decision, we give our special thanks to Mr Md Mustafizur Rahman Khan, learned Advocate appearing before us who lighted us by presenting the law properly.

Communicate this order at once.

End.

full_judgment:
SK Sinha J : This Rule at the instance of the defendant is against an order of the learned District Judge, Khulna in Civil Revision No. 81 of 2005 reversing that dated 12-6-2005 of the learned Joint District Judge, 4th Court, Khulna in Title Suit No. 23 of 2005.

2. This Rule arose out of the following facts: Petitioner instituted Title Suit No. 41 of 1998 in the 4th Court of Subordinate Judge, Khulna against one SM Abdul Hoque and another for declaration of title in respect of the suit properties described in the schedule to the plaint. The suit was decreed on solenama by order dated 29-6-99.The Opposite Parties instituted Title Suit No. 23 of 2005 in the 4th Court of Joint District Judge, Khulna against the petitioner and defendants in Title Suit No. 41 of 1998 for setting aside the sole decree and for partition. In the suit the plaintiff-opposite parties filed an application on 19-3-2005 under section 151, CPC for staying the judgment and decree passed in Title Suit No. 41 of 1998. The learned Joint District Judge allowed the application and stayed the operation of the judgment and decree passed in the earlier suit. Thereafter, on the application of the petitioner, the learned Joint District Judge vacated the order of stay by order dated 12-6-2005. The plaintiff-opposite parties thereafter, moved a revision petition being Civil Revision No. 81 of 2005 before the learned District Judge, Khulna. The learned District Judge by the impugned order set aside the order of the learned Joint District Judge and stayed the judgment and decree passed in Title Suit No. 41 of 1998.

<u>3. It is contended on behalf of the petitioner that the learned Joint District Judge has committed a fundamental error in staying the judgment and decree in failing to notice that the decree that was passed was not executable and therefore, there was no scope for staying the judgment and decree passed in the earlier suit. It is further contended that the plaintiff opposite parties were not parties in the earlier suit and therefore, they could not legally maintain an application for stay of the judgment and decree passed in the earlier suit.</u>

4. As observed above, the petitioner instituted the earlier suit seeking declaration of the simpliciter in the suit lands. The suit was decreed on compromise, in that the plaintiff-opposite parties were not parties and no decree was passed against them as well. The petitioner did not obtain any decree for recovery of khas possession in respect of the suit property. Therefore, there was nothing to be stayed of the judgment and decree passed in the suit. If an executable decree was passed in respect of the properties involved in the subsequent suit the Court may, on such terms as to security or otherwise, as it thinks fit, stay execution of the decree on the prayer of the aggrieved party until the pending suit has been decided.

<u>5. The learned District Judge while staying the judgment and decree passed in Title Suit No. 41 of 1998 observed that whether or not the suit properties were purchased out of the joint income of three brothers, Bahadur Sheikh, Omar Sheikh and SM Abdul Haque would be decided on evidence and since that decree was challenged, if the defendants had transferred the suit lands by way of sale or mortgage there would arise multiplicity of the suits. This finding of the learned District Judge is self-contradictory. If the defendant-petitioner wanted to transfer the suit lands the plaintiffs were left without alternative remedies. The reason on which the order of stay was passed was a misconceived one. Since the decree passed in Title Suit No. 41 of 1998 was not executable the Court had no power to stay the said decree. The learned District Judge had failed to consider that aspect of the matter and erroneously stayed the said decree. Though the learned Joint District Judge committed same error while passing the initial order of stay, but subsequently on the application of the petitioner he had rectified the order and vacated the order of stay. We find error in the order of the learned District Judge in staying the judgment and decree passed in Title Suit No. 41 of 1998 which has occasioned a failure of justice. In view of the above, we find substance in the contention of the learned Advocate for the petitioner, we find merit in this Rule.</u>

<u>In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs. The impugned judgment and order of the learned District Judge is set aside and that of the learned Joint District Judge is restored.</u>

End.

caseno: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 1745 of 2005
lawyer:
Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, Senior Advocate, instructed by Md Aftab Hossnin, Advocate-on-Record -For the Petitioner. 
Mozibur Rahman, Advocate, instructed by Syed Mahbubur Rahman, Advocate-on-Record-For Respondent Nos. 3 & 4. 
Not represented -Respondent Nos. 1, 2 & 5-12.
parties:
Nazibun Nessa Begum ----- Petitioner
Vs.
Asia Begum & others ----- Respondents
case_source: (From the Judgment and Order dated July 11, 2005 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 1387 of 1989)
full_judgment:
Md Ruhul Amin J : This petition for leave to appeal has been filed against the judgment dated July 11, 2005 of a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 1387 of 1989 making absolute the Rule obtained against the judgment and decree dated August 20, 1989 of the 2nd Court of Additional District Judge, Barisal in Title Appeal No. 130 of 1987 dismissing the same and thereby affirming the judgment and decree dated July 19, 1987 of the Court of Assistant Judge passed in Title Suit No. 306 of 1985 dismissing the same. The suit was filed seeking declaration that the proceeding of the VP case mentioned in schedule 'Kha' to the plaint is illegal, fraudulent, collusive and not binding upon the plaintiffs and also for a decree for permanent injunction restraining the defendants from interfering in any way with the plaintiffs' possession in the land described in schedule 'Ka'.

2. The suit was filed stating, inter alia, that Santosh Kumar and Saroj Kumar were the owners of the land in suit and they settled the land with the plaintiff Nos. 1 and 2 in Falgoon 1354 BS and since then they are in possession of the land in suit, that the record of right having not been prepared in their names they were constrained to file Title Suit No. 501 of 1962 in the 1st Court of Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge), Barisal and the same was decreed on December 7, 1962 and on the basis of the said decree plaintiffs got their names mutated in the record of right and paying rent to the Government. The plaintiff Nos. 1 and 2 sold the part of the land in suit to the plaintiff Nos. 3 and 4 in October 1983 and the said plaintiff Nos. 3 and 4 got their names mutated in the Pourashava holding and after obtaining the approved plan constructed buildings taking loan from the House Building Finance Corporation and for the purpose of obtaining loan from the House Building Finance Corporation plaintiff Nos. 3 and 4 mortgaged their share to the said Corporation, that plaintiff Nos. 1 and 2 constructed tin-shed and 'golpata' huts and let out the same, that certain Fakruddin Talukder and others as plaintiffs filed Title Suit No. 375 of 1975 for setting aside the decree passed in Title Suit No. 501 of 1962 and the same was dismissed on contest, that at no point of time the property in suit assumed the character of enemy property, later on vested property and that VP Cases No. 1 of 1985 started on July 20, 1985 treating the land in suit as vested and non-resident property is illegal, fraudulent and void.

3. The suit was contested by the Government alleging, inter alia, that plaintiff Nos. 1 and 2 had no locus standi to file the suit and that the decree obtained in Title Suit No. 501 of 1962 was illegal and void and not binding on the defendants, that plaintiffs' story of taking settlement is not true and the pattan, if any, taken was not legal because of the pro-vision of section 107 of the Transfer of Property Act, that plaintiffs have no right, title and possession in the land in suit, that property in suit was rightly treated as vested property since the owners left the country in 1947 for India and permanently settled there, that the land in suit was leased out to defendant No. 3 who is in possession of the same as lessee of the defendant No. 1, that plaintiffs are claiming the land in suit on the basis of fabricated and manufactured documents and papers. The defendant No. 3 contested the suit by adopting the written statement of the defendant No. 1.

4. The trial Court dismissed the suit on the findings that plaintiffs failed to prove their pattan and the decree obtained in Title Suit No. 501 of 1962 was fraudulent, that plaintiffs and the defendant No. 3 having had found the land as vested property trespassed therein and are in possession thereof. The appellate Court concurred with the findings and decisions of the trial Court and thereupon dismissed the appeal.

<u>5. The plaintiffs then moved the High Court Division in revisional jurisdiction and obtained Rule. The High Court Division, in the background of the frame of the suit, observed that the courts below were not required "to investigate into the title of the parties in detail" but were required to consider the prima facie title of the plaintiff for the purpose of arriving at the finding whether the plaintiffs have locus standi to challenge the proceedings of the vested property case which has been started in 1985, that plaintiff Nos. 1 and 2 obtained decree declaring their title in the land in suit and the said suit was filed impleading the original owners and that on the basis of the decree plaintiffs' names were mutated in 1964 and that subsequent purchasers from the plaintiff Nos. 1 and 2 got their names mutated, that Government realised rent from the plaintiff Nos. 1 and 2 as well as from the plaintiff Nos. 3 and 4 since 1960 till the date, that Pourashava holding stands in the name of the plaintiffs and the plaintiff Nos. 3 and 4 on the basis of plan approved by the Municipality constructed building and thus it is quite evident that the decree obtained in Title Suit 501 of 1962 was acted upon and the Government accepted the plaintiffs as the tenants in respect of the land in suit upon accepting rent, that there are sufficient materials on record to show that plaintiffs are in possession of the land in suit, that as the Government accepted the plaintiffs as tenants of the land in suit and, as such, estopped from questioning the title of the plaintiffs, that Exhibits 8 and 4 series i.e. khatians and rent receipts respectively, clearly show that the plaintiffs have locus standi to file the suit seeking declaration, that the order of the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) treating the property in suit as vested property on July 20, 1985 is illegal, void and collusive that since the plaintiffs have established their locus standi to file the suit seeking declaration against the order treating the property in suit as vested property and, as such, the suit so framed is quite maintainable and the plaintiffs are entitled to the relief sought for, that the law is settled now that with the repeal of Ordinance No. 1 of 1969 with effect from March 23, 1974 no property can be declared as vested and non-resident property after that date and, as such, order dated July 20, 1985 passed by the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Barisal in VP. Case No. 1 of 1985/MP 516 of 1983 is illegal, void and without jurisdiction, that DW 1 has admitted that the property in suit has not been listed in the census list and from the defendants' side no paper was filed to show that the land in suit was treated as vested property in between 6-9-1965 and 16-2-1969 that the defendant No. 3 who figured as DW 2 could not produce any DCR or any paper in support of her being lessee and her claim of being lessee was not supported by any other witness, that the trial Court as well as lower appellate Court while making finding as to the decree obtained in Title Suit No. 501 of 1962 failed to consider Exhibit 8 series and Exhibit 4 series and also overlooked the material fact that the said decree was not challenged by filing a regular suit and no issue was also framed in the suit with regard to the legality and validity of the decree obtained in Title Suit No. 501 of 1962, that the frame of the suit was not for investigation of the title but for investigation as to the legality of the order passed treating the property as vested property, that the trial Court as well as appellate Court lost sight of the fact that the decree obtained in Title Suit No. 501 of 1962 was acted upon since plaintiff's names were mutated in the record of right and rent was received from them, that property in suit was treated as vested property at a time i.e. in the year 1985, when there was no law empowering the Government or the Vested Property authority to treat the property in suit as vested property, that the finding of the trial Court as well as the lower appellate Court that both the parties are in possession of the land in suit is totally incorrect since defendant No. 3 who figured as DW 2 could neither produce any paper in support of his being the lessee of the land in suit, nor any paper showing payment of any rates or levies, that plaintiffs by the evidence of as many as 6 PWs have proved their possession in the land in suit and the oral evidence is being further strengthened by the Exhibit 8 series and Exhibit 4 series and Exhibit 1 series and the Exhibit 'Ka', notice to surrender possession, prove possession of the plaintiffs in the land in suit, that defendant No.1 could not prove possession of its lessee in the land in suit. On the aforesaid finding, the High Court Division made the Rule absolute.</u>

6. The present petition for leave to appeal has been filed by defendant No. 3 who claimed herself as lessee of the Government.

<u>7. The judgment of the High Court Division has not been challenged by the vested property authority. The facts of the instant case demonstrate how the citizen is being harassed by the government functionaries resorting to a proceeding which in the eye of law is totally illegal because of the fact that proceeding treating the property as vested property was started on July 20, 1985 when there was no law for treating the property as vested property. No material was placed from the side of the defendant No. 1 to show that at any time before July 20, 1985 the property was treated as vested property. DW 1 who deposed on behalf of the defendant No. 1 i.e. the vested property authority, could not produce any paper to show that the property was treated as vested property when the law relating to vested property was in operation. The property does not find place in the census list. On the top of other evidence plaintiff Nos. 1 and 2 got their names mutated in the record of right as back as in 1964. This being the position it is quite clear that there was no material before the vested property authority to treat the property in suit as vested property and the vested property authority has initiated the proceeding being influenced by certain interested quarter quite illegally.</u>

8. In the background of the materials on record and the facts and circumstances of the case the learned Counsel for the petitioner finds difficulty to assail the findings and decisions made by the High Court Division while setting aside the judgment and decree of the lower appellate Court affirming the judgment of the trial Court.

9. On perusal of the judgment of the lower appellate Court and the trial Court it is seen that the said Courts did not advert their mind to the frame of the suit and the relief sought in the suit and made the finding as to possession on total non-consideration of the evidence on record.

10. In view of the discussions made hereinbefore, we find no merit in the petition.

Accordingly, the petition is dismissed.

End.

caseno: Appeal from Original Order (FMA) No. 65 of 2008 with Civil Rule No. 555(F)/2007.
lawyer:
Probir Neogi, Advocate—For the Appellants. 
Jamaluddin Ahmed with AKM Shakhawat Hossain, Advocates—For Respondent No. 1.
parties:
Meer Niaz Mohammad ----- Petitioner
vs
Bangladesh Shilpa Rin Sangstha and others ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
SAN Mominur Rahman J : This appeal arises out of the order dated 31-1-2007 passed in Miscellaneous Case No. 1219 of 2005 by the learned District Judge Dhaka, rejecting the prayer for restoration of the case being barred by limitation.

2. The appeal is being contested by the plaintiff decree-holder-respondent BSRS.

3. The plaintiff-decree holder respondent No. 1 hereof filed the suit in order to realise its due money enjoyed by the defendant No. 1 company as loan, for setting up its Industry, secured by the Directors and others including the appellant hereof, and that though the suit was filed under the provisions of Bangladesh Shilpa Rin Sangstha, 1972 (PO 128 of 1972) but wrongly filed in the Court of Artha Rin Adalat No. 2, Dhaka, and that during the pendency of the suit it was detected that the suit was filed in the wrong forum, inasmuch as suit filed by BSRS for realisation of its money with fixed Court Fee prescribed by the BSRS Orders, is required to be filed before the District Judge and that the plaint of the suit was withdrawn from the Court of the learned Subordinate Judge by the learned District Judge, who on receipt of the case on 21-6-1999, registered the said case as Miscellaneous Case No. 348 of 1999 in the Court of District Judge and that the learned District Judge on the same date i.e. on 21-6-1999, without following the procedure as laid down in the said BSRS Order and without issuing any fresh summons fixed the case on 17-8-1999 for ex parte disposal and that on the said date i.e. on 17-8-1999 the case was heard ex parte and the decree was passed for Taka 20,21,9000 as of 1-1-1992, together with interest @ 14.5% on the decretal amount till realisation with further direction to realise the decretal amount by putting the mortgage property in auction sale in accordance with law. It is alleged that the defendant No. 5, who is the appellant herein, came to know about the said decree on 8-10-2002 and on entering appearance by filing power prayed for "permission and time" to file written objection and time was allowed on several occasions thereafter. However, vide order dated 9-8-2005 the written objection as filed was rejected on the ground that the Miscellaneous Case No. 348 of 1999 was decreed earlier and that faced with such circumstances the appellant hereof filed an application under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure for restoration of the case, filing an application for condonation of delay under section 5 of the Limitation Act, contending, amongst others, that the written objection filed earlier was on the wrong advice of the learned Advocate and that the said application for condonation of delay was heard and rejected by the impugned order dated 31-1-07 and consequently the application filed under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure praying for restoration of the case was also rejected being time barred with the observation that the appellant has not given any proof in support of his statement about the wrong advice given by the learned Advocate and on such rejection another application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure was filed but without any success and, as such, there was delay. Being aggrieved, as such, the instant appeal has been preferred.

4. Perused the memo of appeal, the application filed under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the application filed under section 5 of the Limitation Act for condonation of delay filed before the Court below and the order sheet of Miscellaneous Case No. 240 of 1992 of the Court of Artha Rin Adalat No. 2, Dhaka and Miscellaneous Case No. 348 of 1999 of the Court of District Judge, Dhaka and considered the submissions of the learned Advocates of the contesting parties.

5. The learned Advocate appearing for the defendant No. 5 appellant submitted that the learned District Judge erred in law in not providing any opportunity to the appellant to substantiate the case of the appellant as to the condonation, since in the pleading the appellant has taken the plea that because of wrong advice given by his learned Advocate the appellant has filed written objection in the original Miscellaneous Case instead of filing required application under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure for restoration and that as the learned District Judge, as it appears, did not believe the statement of the appellant, as to the wrong advice given by the learned Advocate, though made on oath, he ought to have given an opportunity to prove such statement of the appellant for ends of justice. The learned Advocate further submitted that the learned District Judge ought to have examined the statement made by the appellant petitioner that the miscellaneous case filed under the BSRS Order has been illegally decreed ex parte, without following the mandatory provisions of the BSRS Order relating to the issuance of summons and that the learned District Judge acted illegally in fixing the date of hearing ex parte on the same date he received the case records on transfer from the Artha Rin Adalat, inasmuch as it was mandatory on the part of the District Judge to issue fresh summons, the case being proceeded with on a new procedure on the basis of a special law (BSRS Order) on transfer from the Artha Rin Adalat without notice and thereby the disposal of the miscellaneous case under the BSRS Order as made by the learned District Judge was not in accordance with the law and the same is liable to be set aside. The learned Advocate further submitted that in such circumstances, when the mistake is on the part of the Court itself, the Court is required to exercise its inherent power to give justice by way of ordering restoration of the case as soon as the matter came to its notice. The learned Advocate took us through section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure and also a decision of this Court on the similar issue in the case of Kazi Jawaherul Islam vs Standard Co-operative Credit Society Ltd, reported in 1998 BLD 310 = 50 DLR 333, in support of his aforesaid contention as to the duty of a Court to secure the ends of justice.

6. The learned Advocate then referring to a case of the Supreme Court of India namely Collector Land Acquisition, Anantnag vs Katiji, reported in AIR 1987 SC 1353, submitted that in order to appreciate the words "sufficient causes" in order to condone or not to condone delay as appearing in section 5 of the Limitation Act, due regards have to be given to the facts and circumstances of individual cases. The learned Advocate, in the language of their Lordships in the said case, has submitted that:

"Every day's delay must be explained does not mean that a pedantic approach should be made. Why not every hour's delay, every second's delay?. The doctrine must be applied in a rational common sense pragmatic manner.

When substantial justice and technical considerations are pitted against each other, cause of substantial justice deserves to be preferred for the other side cannot claim to have vested right in injustice being done because of a non-deliberate delay.

There is no presumption that delay is occasioned deliberately, or on account of culpable negligence, or on account of malafides. A litigant does not stand to benefit by resorting to delay. In fact, he runs a serious risk.

It must be grasped that judiciary is respected not on account of its power to legalise injustice on technical grounds but because it is capable of removing injustice and is expected to do so."

7. The learned Advocate lastly submitted that a Court of law is required to give justice and for that matter it is required to be lenient in its approach and the legislature have also accepted this principle and in order to avoid complicity has recently amended the provision of law for restoration of cases disposed of ex parte by adding new provision i.e. rules 9A and 13A in Order IX of the Code of Civil Procedure, which has provided an opportunity for restoration of a case disposed of ex parte, on payment of prescribed fees, of course, against some conditions. The learned Advocate also referred to a decision in the case of BSRS vs Monowara Begurn, reported in 2006 BLD (AD) 276 = 58 DLR (AD) 195, arising out of a case, initially filed by the BSRS for realisation of its outstanding dues in the Court of Subordinate Judge and Artha Rin Adalat No. 2, Dhaka, and subsequently transferred to the Court of the learned District Judge, Dhaka, and their Lordships held that notice issued by Artha Rin Adalat cannot be treated as a notice issued as contemplated by Article 33(1) and (5) of the BSRS Order and the decree passed by the learned District Judge, without issuing notice as per Article 33(1) of the BSRS Order, has been set aside and sent back for fresh decision, on remand, in accordance with law. The learned Advocate for the decree-holder BSRS however submitted that in the meantime about 10 years having been passed after pronouncement of the decree in 1999 and the loan was of 1981 and that there is every reason to believe that the appellant had knowledge about the case filed in 1992 by the BSRS for recovery of its outstanding dues in the Court of Artha Rin Adalat No. 2, Dhaka, more-so when the notice about the case was published in the national daily newspapers, as per order of the Court below. It is asserted that the defendant-appellant has come up lately malafide to delay the realisation of the loan amount.

8. The learned Advocate could not produce any material from the records of the case to show that any notice was issued following the provisions of Article 33 (1) and (5) of the BSRS Order, inasmuch as the suit has been decreed under the BSRS Order. The learned Advocate also found it difficult to meet the contention of the learned Advocate of the appellant to the effect that for ends of justice the learned District Judge, ought to have given an opportunity to prove his case of wrong advice given by his learned Advocate, when such statement was made on oath. The learned Advocate avoided to make any submission on the inherent power of the Court under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure, to secure justice and not to use any technical ground to stop any litigant from seeking justice. We appreciate the manner the learned Advocate for the BSRS has made his submission before a superior Court of the country.

<u>9. It appears from the order No. 93 dated 21-6-1999 and order No. 94 dated 17-8-1999, as contained in the certified copy of the order sheet of Miscellaneous Case No. 240 of 1992 (Artha Rin Adalat-2 Dhaka) and Miscellaneous Case No. 348 of 1999 (District Judge, Dhaka), annexed to the memo of appeal that the case was transferred from the Artha Rin Adalat No. 2, Dhaka, to the Court of District Judge, Dhaka on 21-6-1999 and on that date i.e. on 21-6-1999 the date for exparte hearing was fixed on 17-8-1999 and the suit was heard and decreed exparte on 17-8-1999. Thus it appears that the learned District Judge on receipt of the case records from the Artha Rin Adalat proceeded to dispose of the case under the provisions of BSRS Order but did not take any step to follow the provisions as laid down in Article 33 of the BSRS Order 1972 as to issuance of notice. It further appears that the learned District Judge, has acted without jurisdiction in proceeding with the case without issuing any summons in accordance with the provision of the said BSRS Order, 1972 or issuing any notice informing the defendants about the transfer of the case, and that hits the principle of natural justice and that the fixation of date of ex parte disposal of the case without issuing any notice upon the defendant as per Article 33 of the BSRS Order cannot be said to be in accordance with law.</u>

<u>10. We find substance also in the submission of the learned Advocate appearing for the appellant that the appellant ought to have been given an opportunity to prove his case of wrong advice given by the learned Advocate, which fact the appellant asserted on oath in his pleading, and such act, on the part of the District Judge in not providing an opportunity to a litigant to prove his case, is against natural justice and thus the rejection of condonation application resulting in rejection of the application filed under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure for restoration is illegal and cannot be maintained.</u>

<u>11. We have perused the decisions cited by the learned Advocate for the appellant, with which we are respectfully in agreement. The case of BSRS reported in 2006 BLD (AD) 276, supports the case of the appellant as to the non-compliance of the provision of Article 33 in the issuance of fresh notice and the consequence therefor. The case reported in 1998 BLD 310 supports the case of the appellant to take recourse to inherent power of the Court as provided under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure to secure justice. From the decision of the Indian Supreme Court in the case of Collector, Land Acquisition, Anantnag vs Katiji, reported in AIR 1982 (SC) 1353, we are benefited to get a new approach for giving a liberal meaning in deciding the meaning of "sufficient case" as to delay for the purpose of condonation, wherein it has been rightly observed that "judiciary is respected not on account of its power to legalise injustice on technical grounds but because it is capable of removing injustice and is expected to do so". In the instant case, it was categorically stated that the delay was due to wrong advice of the learned Advocate and that it appeared from the records of case below that the mandatory provisions for issuance of summons under the BSRS Order was not complied with and no notice was issued upon the opposite parties of the case, after receipt of the case records from the Artha Rin Adalat. Therefore, the ex parte disposal of case under the BSRS Order, 1972 as made was not in accordance with law and the learned District Judge ought to have considered such special facts in passing the impugned order rejecting the application for condonation. We are of the view that the learned District Judge proceeded with the application for condonation on wrong approach and thereby arrived at his wrong decision, which has occasioned failure of justice. Thus we find merit in the appeal. However, it appears that because of choosing of the wrong steps, whether on the wrong advice of the learned Advocate or not, the BSRS has, in fact, suffered monetarily. In that view of the matter, we are inclined to allow token compensation in favour of the plaintiff decree-holder BSRS in allowing the appeal.</u>

12. Accordingly the appeal is allowed with cost. The impugned order dated 31-1-2007 passed in Miscellaneous Case No. 1219 of 2005 rejecting the application for condonation of delay, thereby rejecting the application filed under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure, (registered as Miscellaneous Case No. 1219 of 2005) summarily holding to be barred by limitation, are set aside and the Miscellaneous Case No. 1219 of 2005 is allowed on contest and accordingly, the judgment and decree passed in Miscellaneous Case No. 348 of 1999 on 17-8-1999 is set aside and the Miscellaneous Case No. 348 of 1999 is restored to its original file and number, on condition of payment of compensation of Taka 50,000 (fifty thousand) to the BSRS, to which the appellant agreed, within 45 (forty-five) working days of receipt of this order by the District Judge in default the appeal shall stand dismissed. The learned District Judge, in view of passages of time in the meantime, is directed to dispose of the Miscellaneous Case No. 348 of 1999 within 60 (sixty) working days from the date of receipt of this judgment and order. The appellant undertakes not to take any adjournment in the case before the learned District Judge.

The connected Rule being No. 555(FM)/ 2007 is disposed of accordingly.

End.

lawyer:
Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, Senior Advocate, instructed by Sajjadul Huq, Advocate-on-Record—For the Appellant. 
Mozaffer Hossain, Senior Advocate, instructed by Md Nawab Ali, Advocate-on-Record—For the Respondent Nos. 1-3. 
Ex parte— Respondent No. 2
parties:
Hyder Ali Mia (Md)  ----- Appellant
Vs.
Razia Begum and others ----- Respondents
case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 4-7-1994 passed by the High Court Division in First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 696 of 1991)
full_judgment:
Md. Tafazzul Islam J: This appeal by leave has arisen out of the judgment and order dated 4-7-1994 passed by the High Court Division in First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 696 of 1991 allowing the appeal upon setting aside judgment and order dated 26-8-1991 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge), Bogra in Miscellaneous Case No. 13 of 1987 by which the ex park judgment and decree dated 13-3-1986 passed in Other Class Suit No. 46 of 1986 was set aside and thereby the above suit was restored to its original file and number.

2. The appellant instituted the above suit for specific performance of contract and on obtaining ex parte decree dated 10-3-1986 got a sale deed executed and registered in his favour through Court in Other Class Execution Case No. 6 of 1986; subsequently, the defendant No. 1 filed Miscellaneous Case No. 13 of 1987 under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the above ex parte decree on the grounds that the summons was not served upon her and that on 19-6-1985, i.e. before service of summons, she left Bangladesh for her father's residence at Peshawar in Pakistan and her husband, defendant No. 2, was untraceable since December, 1985. The plaintiff contested the above miscellaneous case asserting that summons were duly served upon the defendants and the notices were also sent upon the defendants by registered post which being refused by the defendants, according to law, were deemed to have been served upon the defendants. The learned Subordinate Judge (now joint District Judge), Bogra dismissed the above miscellaneous case on the findings, inter alia, that Ext 'Ka' series show that the summons of the suit were duly served upon the defendants through process server and OPW No. 3, the attesting witness, proved service of summons while the defendants failed to prove that no summons were served upon them and moreover, the defendants did not challenge the service of summons which were sent through registered post and sending of summons through registered post has got strong legal presumption of service under section 27 of the General Clauses Act; it is an admitted fact that the husband of the defendant No. 1 sometime in the year 1985 took shelter in the residence of his brother Md Rafiq Khan whose residence is situated at Sutrapur, Bogra Town, Bogra and therefore, the address of the defendants given in the plaint were correct address and services of summons were made in that address; the allegation of not knowing the whereabouts of Abdur Rashid Khan, the husband of the defendant No. 1, is nothing but myth and altogether disproved by evidence; the said Md Abdur Rashid Khan was made party in the miscellaneous case as opposite party No. 3 and notices were duly served upon him through court and also by registered post and, as such, evidently he is not untraced; since the summons were evidently served upon the defendant No.1 and yet she did not appear to contest the suit, the suit was rightly decreed ex parte. Being aggrieved, the defendants filed the above miscellaneous appeal before the High Court Division and after hearing allowed the appeal.

3. Leave was granted on the submissions that the High Court Division erred in holding that the summons were not served upon defendant No. 1 as there was no tender of the same upon her and that the High Court Division overlooked the provisions of rule 15 of Order V and also rule 3 of Order III of the Code of Civil Procedure, and since summons sent by registered post was also returned with the postal peon's endorsement of 'refusal' by the defendants, the High Court Division erred in holding that the said notices were not duly served.

4. The learned Counsel for the appellant submits that the summons having been issued on both defendant Nos. 1 and 2 and the process server having served the summons on defendant No. 2 as the agent of defendant No. 1 and also on the defendant No. 2 personally and the process server, the OPW No. 2, also having deposed that he has served the summons on the defendants at the address written on the summons and OPW No. 3, the attesting witness, having also attested the service of summons in terms of the provisions of rules 9 to 19 of Order V and rule 3 of Order III of the Code of Civil Procedure, it will be deemed that the summons were duly served and further the summons being duly sent by registered post with acknowledgment duly addressed to defendant Nos. 1 and 2 in accordance with the provisions laid down in rule 19B, Order V Code of Civil Procedure and said summons having been returned with the endorsement made by the postal peon as being 'refused', there was also proper service of the summons sent by registered post and therefore, the High Court Division committed error in holding that the provision of rule 19B of Order V has not been complied with.

<u>5. As it appears the High Court Division found that to prove the service of summons the plaintiff examined OPW No. 2, the process-server and the OPW No. 3, the attesting witness, and as is evident from the report of the process server, he went to the residence of the defendant No. 1 and when the husband of defendant No. 1 refused to accept the summons it was served by hanging but the contents of the summons show that the process server was directed to cause service of summons on two defendants, the defendant No.1 as well as the defendant No. 2, her husband, but the service return does not indicate that the process server attempted to cause service of summons on defendant No. 2; the process server, while deposing as OPW 2, in his examination-in-chief, stated that he has served the summons on the defendants but did not state on oath that he tried to serve the summons on both the defendants and when they refused to accept the same those were served by hanging; further, the process server is also completely silent on the mode of service of summons or attempted service of summons on defendant No. 2 and if his evidence is considered it would appear that the summons were served only on the defendant No.1 though, as a matter of fact, there were two defendants; moreover, OPW 3, the attesting witness, on service of summons, in his examination-in-chief stated that the process server served the summons upon Abdur Rashid Khan, the defendant No. 2 in his presence but this OPW No. 3 did not state a single word on the service of summons on defendant No. 1 and though the records show that after the receipt of the return the trial Court fixed a date for ex parte disposal but before fixing the date, the trial Court has not looked into the service return; the records of the trial Court does not show that the provision of rule 19B of Order V of the Code of Civil Procedure has been complied with and even in the records there is no material showing sending of the summons by registered post with acknowledgment due and there is also nothing on record to indicate that the postal acknowledgment due was received by the trial Court and no step was also taken by the respondent to examine the postal peon to prove the service of summons which was sent by registered post with A / D; in the case of Abul Khair Mia vs. Abdul Latif Sardar reported in 32 DLR (AD) 167 it has been held that an ex parte decree obtained by suppressing summons is a decree obtained fraudulently and, as such, nullity and the decree, which has been questioned in the present miscellaneous appeal, is a nullity; in the present case in a hot haste an ex parte decree was obtained which indicates that a fraud was committed upon the court as well as upon the defendants and in 32 DLR (AD) 167 as referred above the Appellate Division also held that when a fraud is proved then there is no question of limitation and time will run from the date when the fraud is detected and so the question of limitation does not arise in the present case; even if, for argument's sake, it is conceded that the fraud was detected earlier, even then the Court is not debarred to interfere under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure and in the case of Mofazzal Molla and another vs. Parul Bala Debi and others reported in 24 DLR 78 it has been held been that in a case where fraud is committed upon the Court as well as upon the party, a Court has inherent jurisdiction to interfere in the matter in exercising its power vested in section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure and similar view has also been expressed in the case of Mozaffar Ahmed and others vs. Moulvi Salah Ahmed and others reported in 40 DLR 239; Amir Hossain Sardar vs. Sarat Chandra and others reported in 31 DLR 109 and Master Abdul Aziz vs. Abani Mohan Mukherjee and others reported in 30 DLR (AD) 221.</u>

<u>We are of the view that the High Court Division, on proper assessment of the materials on record and applying the principle of law as applicable in the present appeal, arrived at a correct decision and there is no cogent reason to interfere with the above decision. So, the appeal is dismissed without any order as to costs.</u>

End.

full_judgment:
This Rule arises out of the judgment and decree dated 29-10-2002 passed by the Joint District Judge, Second Court, Kurigram, in other Appeal No.63 of 1998, preferred against the judgment and decree dated 15-7-1998 passed by the Senior Assistant Judge, Ulipur, Kurigram, in Other Suit No. 128 of 1995.

2. The petitioners as plaintiffs instituted the suit for declaration that the enlistment of the suit property described in schedule 'Ka' and 'Kha' appended to the plaint as vested and nonresident property is void, illegal, inoperative, without jurisdiction. During pendency of the suit by amending plaint they asked for further declaration of their title in the suit land in the newly added schedule 'Ga' which is situated within the land of schedule 'Ka' and 'Kha' and also for recovery of khas possession since from that land they were allegedly dispossessed during the pendency of the suit.

3. The plaint of the plaintiffs is, in brief, that the suit property described in schedule 'Ka' and 'Kha' of the plaint originally belonged to Ambika Charan Sarker who died leaving behind 3 sons namely, Kali Charan Sarker, Upendra Nath Sarker and Nripendra Nath Sarker, as his heirs and successors in the suit land. Thereafter Kali Charan Sarker died without any issue and his other two brothers Upendra Nath Sarker and Nripendra Nath Sarker became the owners of the suit land. The RS record was prepared in the names of the said 3 (three) brothers. Thereafter, Nripendra Nath Sarker died leaving behind his only brother Upendra Nath Sarker who became the sole owner of the suit land. While Upendra Nath Sarker had been enjoying and possessing the suit land by paying rents to the Government after its mutation in his name died leaving behind the plaintiffs as his legal heirs and successors. The plaintiffs have been enjoying and possessing the suit land. The Settlement Officer on 10-4-1993 refused to record the suit land in the names of the plaintiffs in the recent Khatian saying that the suit land has been listed as vested and nonresident property and vide VP Case No.4 of 1970 it has been leased out to the father of defendant No.3 Fazal Uddin. Hence they instituted the suit for a declaration that enlistment of the suit land as enemy and vested property as illegal.

4. Subsequently by amending the plaint the plaintiffs sought for further declaration of their title in the suit land as well as for recovery of khas possession in respect of a part of the suit land (schedule 'Ga') from where they were allegedly dispossessed by force by the defendant No.3 during pendency of the suit.

5. The defendant No. 1 the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) cum Custodian, Vested and Non Resident Property, Kurigram along with the defendant No.2, Assistant Commissioner (Land), Ulipur, Kurigram filed joint written statement and the defendant No.3 Fazal Uddin separately filed another written statement and contested the suit. The contentions of both the written statements are common. As per the written statements, the successors of the SA recorded tenants left this country for India in 1965 and have been residing there as Indian citizens, accordingly the suit land was enlisted as vested and nonresident property. Thereafter the suit land was leased out to the father of the defendant No.3 vide VP Case No.4 of 1970. After death of his father the defendant No.3 Fazal Uddin has been enjoying and possessing the suit land by paying lease money. The defendant No.3 constructed his homestead over suit plot Nos.199 and 200 and has been cultivating the land of suit Plot No.198, and hence the suit is liable to be dismissed.

6. During trial the learned Assistant Judge framed five issues in the suit that whether (i) the suit is maintainable, (ii) the suit is barred by limitation, (iii) the suit suffers from defect of parties, (iv) whether the plaintiffs have got right, title and interest in the suit land and (v) whether the plaintiffs are entitled to get the relief as prayed for. After hearing the parties the learned Assistant Judge dated 15-7-1998 decreed the suit deciding all the issues in favour of the plaintiffs.

7. The defendant Nos. 1 and 2 i.e. the vested property authority, did not prefer any appeal against the said judgment and decree. But only the defendant No.3 Md Fazal Uddin preferred other Appeal No.63 of 1998 in the Court of District Judge, Kurigram and the plaintiffs also filed a cross objection under Order XLI, rule 22 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The said appeal and cross objection were heard together by the learned Joint District Judge, Second Court, Kurigram who by the impugned judgment and decree dismissed the appeal as well as rejected the cross objection by the impugned judgment and decree.

8. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the impugned judgment and decree so far it relates to their cross objection, the plaintiffs as petitioners moved this Court in revision and obtained the Rule, but no revision was prefer-red by the vested property authority or by the defendant No.3 Md Fazal Uddin.

9. Mr Probir Neogi, learned Advocate appears for the petitioners, and on the other side none appears for the opposite parties.

10. Mr Probir Neogi, the learned Advocate, placed the judgment of the courts below. On perusal of the judgment of the Trial Court it appears that the Trial Court decreed the suit deciding all the issues framed in the suit in favour of the plaintiffs, but in the ordering portion of the judgment he did not mention anything about the prayer of the plaintiffs for recovery of khas possession for which the plaintiffs filed the cross objection. From the judgment of the Trial Court it appears that though all the issues framed were decided in favour of the plaintiffs but inadvertently omitted to write any order in respect of the prayer for recovery of khas possession. On perusal of the judgment of the Appellate Court it appears to me as a peculiar one. The Appellate Court itself found that the appeal preferred by the defendant No. 3 is not maintainable and the defendant No.3 has no locus standi to prefer the appeal. With such finding the Appellate Court decided the appeal and disallowed the same, but even then set aside the judgment and decree passed by the Trial Court and dismissed the suit. Though the appellate Court dismissed the appeal but found that the plaintiffs are not entitled to get decree in respect of the entire suit land rather, they are entitled to get decree in respect of a part of the suit land, as per the Appellate Court no decree in respect of the area mentioned in respect of schedule 'Ga' can be granted in the instant suit, for such decree plaintiff is required to file a proper suit in other form. Such contradictory findings of the appellate Court reveals its no exercise of judicial mind. Mr Neogi, further submits that the appeal as disposed of by the appellate Court cannot be treated as a judgment in an appeal in the eye of law. As per him, an appeal is nothing but a complaint made by the aggrieved party to the higher Court authorised to hear the appeal for setting aside the judgment by which he is aggrieved. In support of his contention, he cited the decision in the case of Nagendra Nath Dey vs Suresh Chandra Dey reported in AIR 1932 (Privy Council) 165. In respect of the omission of the Trial Court in his ordering portion regarding the prayer of the plaintiffs for recovery of khas possession Mr Neogi submits that practically the suit was decreed with the declaration of the title of the plaintiffs in the land described in schedule 'Ga' of the plaint which is part of schedule 'Ka' and 'Kha' and also with decree for recovery of khas possession of that part from which the plaintiffs were dispossessed during pendency of the suit and mere omission of writing the order for recovery of khas possession or declaration of title in respect of a part of the suit land in ordering portion of the judgment of the Trial Court will not operate as refusal of such reliefs prayed by the plaintiffs. In support of his contention he cited the decision in the case of, Bangladesh Steel Mills Ltd. vs Masud Reza, reported in 30 DLR (SC) 169.

<u>11. Hearing the learned Advocate for the petitioners and perusal of the record along with the decisions cited above I hold the view that the judgment delivered by the trial Court cannot be treated as a judgment by a court of law. Moreover, admittedly three sons of original CS recorded tenant Ambika Charan Sarker succeeded their father's property, ultimately the suit land devolved upon the predecessor of the plaintiffs, and this fact was admitted by the contesting defendants also. It is also apparent from the judgment of the Trial Court that the vested property authority hopelessly failed to prove the suit land was enlisted as vested property. Particularly, the Government failed to produce any gazette notification notifying the suit land as vested property or census list to show the suit land as enemy property. Rather the orders passed in the alleged vested property case in 1993 were produced before the Court, which are nothing but illegal in the eye of law since in 1993 no property can be declared or enlisted as vested property. I hold further view that, since the vested property authority did not prefer any appeal or revision against the judgment of the Trial Court, meaning that they are not aggrieved with the decision of the trial Court rather they conceded with the decision of the trial Court, the defendant No.3 claiming himself as lessee under vested property authority though he failed to prove such lease by submitting any document of granting such lease has got no locus standi to file the appeal. He is stepping in the shoes of his lessor but the lessor did not come forward to prefer any appeal or revision, meaning that the lessor conceded with the judgment of the Trial Court or with the claim of the plaintiffs. I further hold the view that the plaintiffs asked for further decree for declaration of the title as well as of recovery of khas possession from which they were dispossessed by the defendant No. 3 forcibly during pendency of the suit and on payment of proper court fees the plaintiff by amending the plaint prayed for further decree of recovery of khas possession, and the suit was decreed, but nothing was mentioned in the ordering portion of the judgment of the Trial Court, such omission is nothing but a mere clerical mistake made inadvertently, and, as such, the judgment and decree of the Trial Court will be treated as a decree also for declaration of title to the plaintiffs in the land described in schedule 'Ga' as well as for recovery of its khas possession.</u>

<u>12. With such findings, the Rule is hereby made absolute. Consequently, the impugned judgment and decree dated 29-10-2002 passed by the Joint District Judge, Second Court, Kurigram, in Other Appeal No.63 of 1998 are hereby get aside and the judgment and decree dated 15-7-1998 passed by the Senior Assistant Judge, Ulipur, Kurigram, in other Suit No.128 of 1995 are hereby restored with the modification to the effect the title of the plaintiffs over the land described in schedule 'Ga' of the plaintiff is hereby declared and they are entitled to get recovery of khas possession of the same and the defendants are hereby directed to restore the possession of that land to the plaintiffs within 1 (one) month from the date of receipt of the copy of this judgment, failing which the plaintiff will get possession of the same through Court.</u>

Send down the lower court record immediately.

End.
