full_judgment:
A.B.M. Khairul Haque, J: This first miscellaneous appeal arises out of the judgment and order dated 26-1-1995 passed by the Subordinate Judge, Second Court, Chittagong in Miscellaneous Case No. 158 of 1994, allowing the miscellaneous case filed under Order XXI rule 58 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

2. The facts leading to the filing of this first miscellaneous appeal are that one Zanak Enterprise, the respondent, in response to a notice, published on 26-2-1989, purchased a trawler in an open auction from Bangladesh Fisheries Development Corporation (BFDC) at a price of Taka 3,30,000/- and also obtained possession of the same but suddenly on 17-8-1989, the police seized the said vessel, that on enquiry from the Court, they could learn that a criminal case had been filed by the decree-holder. Thereafter, they filed an application in the Money Execution Case No. 79 of 1984 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, Second Court, Chittagong, under Order XXI, rule 58 of the Code on 19-8-1984. Initially, this was treated as an application, subsequently, since 8-9-1994; this was numbered as Miscellaneous Case No. 158 of 1994. In the said miscellaneous case Ms AK Khan and Co., the decree-holder appellant filed a written objection on 27-9-1994, contending, inter alia, that the trawler in dispute, namely, Taiko Maru No. 5, along with three other trawlers were under attachment since 5-6-1981 firstly, in the Money Suit No. 114 of 1981, in which suit they obtained a decree for Taka 82,84,874.34/- on 19-1-1982 and thereafter in their Money Execution Case No. 79 of 1984. In due course, the said trawler was sold out in open auction and was also delivered in their favour on 17-8-1989. As such, the application under Order XXI, rule 58 of the Code is not maintainable.

3. At the time of hearing of the miscellaneous case, evidence was led both on behalf of the third party petitioner as well as on behalf of the decree-holder purchaser. The learned Judge on consideration of the evidence on record found that the concerned trawler was not attached on 16-3-1989 in the Money Execution Case No. 79 of 1984 filed by the decree-holder and that before such alleged attachment, the petitioner-respondent obtained ownership in the said trawler and that the papers regarding auction and sale were mere paper transaction and was never acted upon. On these findings the learned Judge allowed the miscellaneous case under Order XXI, rule 58 of the Code filed by the 3rd party respondent and released the disputed trawler Taiko Maru No. 5 from attachment and auction sale by his Order dated 26-1-1995. Being aggrieved the decree holder first obtained a Rule under section 115 of the Code on 6-6-1995 but subsequently, on the prayer of the petitioner the Rule was converted into first miscellaneous appeal by order of this Court dated 4-6-2001, converting the Civil Revision No. 2044 of 1995 in the present appeal.

4. Mr. T. H. Khan, Senior Advocate, appears with Mr AB Mahmudul Haque, Advocate, on behalf of the decree-holder-opposite party appellant while Dr. Rafiqur Rahman, Senior Advocate, appears with Mr. Md. Ismail, Advocate, on behalf of the third party petitioner-respondent.

5. Mr. T. H Khan, learned Advocate, appearing on behalf of the appellant, assails the order dated 26-1-1995 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge allowing the miscellaneous case filed under Order XXI, rule 58 of the Code mainly on the ground that once in compliance of the provisions of Order XXI, the sale of the property in auction becomes final as it happened in this case, followed by delivery of possession by the jimmadar on 17-8-1989, in compliance of the direction of the Court, the objection raised at a belated stage on 19-8-1989 purportedly under Order XXI, rule 58 has got no manner of application and was misconceived. Besides he submits that even on the showing of the third party in the said miscellaneous case that they purchased the trawler, namely, Taiko Maru No. 5, and not Taiko Maru No. 5, which would be evident from the execution of the receipt dated 18-3-1989 (Ext. 1) by their seller, Bangladesh Fisheries Development Corporation, as such, their purchased trawler being a different one, they could not have any interest in the trawler, namely, Taiko Maru No. 5.

6. On the other hand, Dr. Rafiqur Rahman, the learned Advocate, appearing on behalf of the third party respondent, submits that they on good faith purchased the concerned trawler from a Government statutory corporation, being Bangladesh Fisheries Development Corporation, being the highest bidder in an open tender at a consideration of Taka 3.30,000/- and thereafter, also incurred huge expenditure in salvaging the same from underneath the mud and to make it seaworthy. He however concedes that what they purchased initially was the trawler Taiko Maru No. 5 but subsequently, the said name was changed to Taiko Maru No. 5 by the seller themselves, on the contention that earlier the name of the trawler was written mistakenly which was a mere typographical mistake made in the plaint and since they obtained the ownership and possession they are entitled to maintain this miscellaneous case and the learned Judge rightly found that the trawler Taiko Maru No. 5 was never under attachment by order of any Court. As such, he prays for dismissal of the appeal.

7. We have heard the learned Advocates of both the sides and also perused the relevant papers on record. It appears that the episode in this case started with the filing of the suit on behalf of A.K. Khan & Company Ltd. against M/s Puso and Company and two others being Money Suit No. 114 of 1981, in the Court of Subordinate Judge, Third Court, Chittagong, on 27-5-1981, praying for a decree for recovery of money and damages for Taka 82, 84,874.34/-. On the next day they also filed an application under Order XXXVIII, rule 5 of the Code, praying for attachment before judgment of the following vessels, namely, (1) Taiko Maru No. 2, (2) Taiko Maru No. 5(3) Trawler Akitso Maru No. 11 and (4) Kyoshine Maru No. 21. Those vessels were in the safe custody of Harbour Master of Chittagong. The Court on hearing the plaintiff petitioner by its order dated 5-6-1981, attached those trawlers lying in the Karnafully River in front of Ralli Ghat at Bangla Bazar, Chittagong and the bailiff of the Court put the said trawlers under the custody of the Harbour Master. In due course, the suit was decreed ex parte on 19-1-1982 against Puso and Company, defendant No. 1, Nonaka Sangyo Company Ltd, defendant No. 2 and Bangla Marine Products Ltd, defendant No. 4. The trawlers which were under attachment, belonged to defendant Nos. 1, 2 and 3. The defendant No. 4 was an associate of the defendant No. 2. Thereafter an execution case being Money Execution Case No. 8 of 1983 was filed on 22-6-1983, to execute the decree for Taka 82, 84,874.34/- obtained by the plaintiff appellant against the aforementioned defendant judgment debtors. This execution case was renumbered as Money Execution Case No. 79 of 1984 on being transferred to the Court of Subordinate Judge, Second Court, Chitttagong. In the said execution case the name of the following trawlers were mentioned, namely, (1) FT Kyeshin Maru No. 21, registration No. 83225 (2) FT Taiko Maru No. 5, registration No. 10971, (3) FT Akitsu Maru No. 11, registration No. 67161. In due course those trawlers mentioned in the petition for execution, was attached under Order XXI, rule 30 on 16-3-1989. Subsequently, notices were published in different news-papers for sale of those trawlers in public auction on 30-4-1989. In due course, the auction of the trawlers. Taiko Maro No. 5 and Akitsu Maru No. 11 was finally held on 30-7-1989 and the decree holder itself purchased the concerned trawlers at a consideration of Taka 17, 65,000/-. Thereafter the decree holder after paying the sale fee, applied for delivery of possession in their favour and the Court by its order dated 15-8-1989 directed the jimmadar of the attached trawler to deliver the possession of those two trawlers in favour of the decree holder auction purchaser. The said order of the Court was communicated to the jimmadar vide memo No. 403 dated 16-8-1989. Accordingly, the jimmadar, one Ferozul Quader Khan, handed over the physical possession of those two trawlers including Taiko Maru No. 5 on 17-8-1989 in favour of one Shawkat Hossain, the representative of the decree-holder and informed the Court by his application dated 20-8-1989.

8. On the other hand, Bangladesh Fisheries Development Corporation (BFDC) filed a suit on 28-3-1983 being Money Suit No. 18 of 1983 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, First Court, Chittagong, against Bangla Marine Products Ltd contending, inter alia, that the defendant company used to avail the harbour facilities from the plaintiff for berthing over and supply of electricity to their fishing vessels, namely, Taiho Maru No. 2 and Taiho Maru No. 3 at the harbour of the plaintiff for a period from 5-5-1978 to 2-11-1979, but the defendant paid their dues up to 30th June, 1978 and took away their vessels, one after the other, without paying the monthly bills towards the berthing and electricity charges, leaving their another vessel, namely, Taiho Maru No. 5, in the harbour situated in the southern bank of river Karnaphuli, under PS Bandar. But when they failed to repay their dues the plaintiff BFDC filed the instant suit claiming the decree for Taka 3, 28,708.19/-. The suit was renumbered as Money Suit No. 70 of 1983. The plaintiff BFDC in the said suit subsequently filed an application on 21-6-1983 under Order XXXVIII, rule 5 of the Code praying for attachment of the vessel, namely, Taiho Maru No. 5. The Court by its Order No. 12 dated 26-7-1983 allowed the prayer for attachment before judgment of the above mentioned trawler. In the meantime, the suit was again re-numbered as Money Suit No. 1163 of 1984 on being transferred to the Court of Subordinate Judge, Second Court. The plaintiff BFDC filed another application on 6-9- 1988 before the Court praying for selling of the said vessel in auction. Accordingly, by Order No. 42 dated 27-9-1988, the learned Judge allowed the prayer for sale in auction of the said vessel and to deposit the sale proceeds in Court. In due course, the auction sale notice was published on 26-2-1989 and the Zanak Enterprise, the third party respondent, purchased the said trawler, namely, Taiho Maru No. 5 vide a money receipt dated 18-3-1989. After such purchase they on salvaging the said trawler found that the name of the said trawler is not Taiho Maru No. 5 but Taiko Maru No. 5. Accordingly, a discrepancy in the name of their purchased trawler cropped up. Thereafter, record shows that the plaintiff BFDC filed two applications on 13-9-1989, one for amendment of the plaint under Order VI, rule 17 read with section 151 of the Code and another application was filed for amendment of the relevant applications, praying for sale of the concerned vessel. The purpose of both the petitions was to amend the name of the concerned trawler, Taiho Maru No. 5, which was earlier sold to the respondent on 18-3-1989, to that of Taiko Maru No. 5, which was under attachment since 5-6-1981 in Money Suit No. 114 of 1981. The Court by Order No. 60 dated 3-9-1989 allowed the amendment of the plaint and also the other applications, such as, application under Order XXXVIII, rule 5, for attachment of the vessel, namely, Taiho Maru No. 5 and another application for sale of the said vessel in auction.

9. At that time, had the learned Second Subordinate Judge, considered the matter closely, he could have found that the alleged inadvertence to mention the name of the trawler Taiho Maru No. 5 instead of Taiko Maru No. 5 was not due to typographical error as alleged in paragraphs 8 and 9 of their petition for amendment of the plaint, rather, the auction purchaser Zanak Enterprise discovered that although the name of the vessel they purchased was Taiho Maru No. 5 but they got another vessel namely, Taiko Maru No. 5 as stated in paragraph 7 of their petition for amendment of the petitions dated 21-6-1983 and dated 6-8-1988, praying for attachment and sale respectively of the vessel Taiho Maru. Perusal of those two applications dated 13-9-1989 for amendment of the name of  the vessel would unmistakably show that the plaintiff BFDC made those two applications for amendment of the name of the vessel not because of their discovery of their alleged mistake in the official records, rather, they did so on the information given to them by the auction purchaser. But they being total strangers to the earlier transitions and business relationship between the BFDC and the defendant, Bangla Marine Products Ltd were not at all in a position to know as to which vessel was left by the defendant at the jetty of the BFDC. Rather, the letters of the BFDC dated 4-3-1989 (Ext. 2ka in Misc. Case No. 158 of 1994) and dated 19-3-1989 (Ext. 2 in Misc. Case No. 158 of 1994) addressed to Zanak Enterprise, would unmistakably show that the vessel Taiho Maru No. 5 was sold in auction to them and not the vessel Taiko Maru No. 5. This will become all the more clear from the receipt dated 18-3-1989 (Ext. 1) given by the BFDC to Zanak Enterprise for an amount of Taka 3, 30,000/- towards the price for the vessel Taiho Maru No. 5.

10. The learned Judge, in allowing the seemingly innocent applications for amendment could not visualise that by those amendments, a different vessel was purported to be attached and sold in auction other than the vessel mentioned in the original plaint itself and the subsequent petitions, dated 21-6-1983 and 6-8-1988 praying for attachment and sale respectively, of the vessel, Taiho Maru No. 5. The records, however, do not show that the auction notice for sale of Taiho Maru No. 5 was also amended. It is apparent that the learned Judge could not visualise the impact of the petitions for amendment and without proper consideration of the nature of the proposed amendments, were illegally allowed. That was the beginning of the confusion.

11. It is apparent from the resume of the facts stated above that the concerned trawler was under attachment of the Court since 5-6-1981 firstly, under Order XXXVIII, rule 5 of the Code on the prayer of the plaintiff in Money Suit No. 114 of 1981, thereafter in pursuance of the provisions of Order XXI of the Code in Money Execution Case No. 78 of 1984, the concerned trawler along with other trawlers were attached on 16-3-1989. As such, it is apparent that M/s Zanak Enterprise, the third party respondent, purchased the trawler Taiho Maru No. 5 by money receipt dated 18-3-1989 from the plaintiff of Money Suit No. 1163 of 1984 and not Taiko Maru No. 5. As such, the question of purchasing the said vessel by them does not arise in spite of the illegal amendment of the name by an order dated 23-9-1989.

The respondent Zanak Enterprise purchased the vessel Taiho Maru No. 5 and not the vessel Taiko Maru No. 5, as such, it has no claim of ownership on the said vessel and the miscellaneous case filed under Order XXI, rule 58 ought to have been rejected.

12. Even if it is assumed that Zanak Enterprise purchased Taiko Maru No. 5 but the said vessel was already under attachment of the Court since 5-6-1981, in MS Suit No. 114 of 1981 and then again was attached in connection with Money Execution Case No. 79 of 1984 on 16-3-1989. Besides, it is also apparent from the records that the physical possession of the trawler Taiko Maru No. 5 had already been handed over in favour of the decree-holder AK Khan and Co on 17-8-1989 by Firojul Kader Khan, the jimmader, in pursuance of the orders of the Court dated 15-8-1989 in the execution proceedings in the Execution Case No. 79 of 1984, filed by AK Khan & Co., the decree-holder petitioner, regarding sale in auction of the concerned trawlers.

13. The provision of rules 74 to 81 under Order XXI of the Code deals with sale of movable property in execution of decrees and orders. Rule 77 envisages the sale of movable property by public auction and when such sale becomes absolute. Rule 77 reads as follows:

"77(1) Where movable property is sold by public auction the price of each lot shall be paid at the time of sale or as soon after as the officer or other person holding the sale directs, and in default of payment the property shall forthwith be re-sold...

(2) On payment of the purchase-money, the officer or other person holding the sale shall grant a receipt for the same, and the sale shall become absolute."

(3)....................................................

"From the plain reading of the above provision it is clear that the moment the purchaser pays the purchase money, the sale becomes absolute under sub-rule (2) and no further formal order of the Court is required as in the case of a sale of immovable property under rule 92 of Order XXI.

14. In the instant case, AK Khan & Co., the decree-holder obtained a decree for Taka 82,84,874.34/-. Four trawlers including Taiko Maru No. 5 were under attachment firstly, since 5-6-1981 under Order XXXVIII, rule 5 in Money Suit No. 114 of 1981 and thereafter the Court, in Money Execution Case No. 79 of 1984, by its Order dated 9-3-1989, issued an order of attachment which was returned after service on 22-3-1989. In due course, the decree-holder filed an application on 20-7-1989 praying for participation in the auction sale to be held on 30-7-1990 which was allowed by the Court. On that date, on the prayer of the decree-holder, the time of 15 days was allowed to file sale-fee and accordingly, the decree-holder submitted court-fees of Taka 17,750/- towards sale-fees on 14-8-1989 and the auction on its behalf was accepted by the Court on that date. On the next date, on 15-8-1989, on the prayer of the decree -holder, the Court ordered release of the trawler from attachment and directed the jimmader to hand over the auctioned property in favour of the decree-holder-auction purchaser. This Order of the Court was communicated to the jimmader by Memo No. 403 dated 16-8-1989. The jimmader, accordingly, handed over the trawler in favour of the decree-holder-auction-purchaser on 17-8-1989.

<u>15. It is palpably clear that in the morning on 17-8-1989 when the trawler namely, Taiko Maru No. 5 was handed over by the jimmadar to the auction purchaser decree holder the whole proceedings came to an end. Even prior to that date, the auction sale of the trawler which is a movable property, as envisaged under the various provisions of Order XXI has reached its finality on 14-8-1989 when the decree holder auction purchaser paid the sale-fees. As such, the contention of Mr TH Khan, the learned Advocate that after finalisation of the sale in auction it cannot be challenged in-a proceeding under Order XXI, rule 58 has got substance. On payment of the sale-fees on 14-8-1989 and after actual delivery of possession of the vessel on 17-8-1989 whole proceedings of the execution, started with the attachment, followed by auction and thereafter sale, reached its finality and cannot be re-opened under any of the provisions of Order XXI not to speak of under rule 58, because Rule 58 envisages an investigation as to the claim of the petitioner, who is a stranger to the suit, during the pendency of attachment made in the execution case and not thereafter when the concerned property had already been released from such attachment. In this case, it is apparent that on 19-8-1989, when the miscellaneous case was filed there was no existence of any attachment; the concerned vessels had already been sold in auction and was physically handed over to the decree-holder-auction-purchaser. In that view of the matter also the miscellaneous case filed under Order XXI, rule 58 of the Code, praying for release of the trawler, namely, Taiko Maru No. 5 from attachment was misconceived and was not maintainable and was liable to be rejected.</u>

16. In the result, the appeal is allowed and the judgment and order passed in the miscellaneous case is set aside.

17. Let a copy of this judgment be forwarded to the learned Judge wherever he is posted now for his future guidance.

Send down the lower Court records forthwith.

End.

full_judgment:
The Rule was issued at the instance of the plaintiff on the following terms:

"Let the records be called for and issue a Rule calling upon the opposite parties to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and decree dated 13-7-1994 passed by the Subordinate Judge, Munshiganj in Title Appeal No. 3 of 1991 should not be set aside and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper."

2. The plaint case, in short, is that the plaintiff instituted Title Suit No. 60 of 1988 in the court of Assistant Judge, Munshiganj for declaration that Memo No. 493 of VP Case No. 121 of 1974 issued by the defendant No. 2 on 11-7-1974 is illegal, void and not binding upon the plaintiff contending, inter alia, that the disputed jama of 0.67 acres consisted of 2 plots appertaining to CS Khatian No. 227 and SA Khatian Nos. 155 and 0.67 acres consisted of 2 plots appertaining to CS Khatian No. 247 and SA 181 under Tajpur Mouza Police Station Sirajdikhan, District Munshiganj was recorded in the name of Tarachand, Gope Chand and Modan Mohan Nath of Khatian No. 227 and Baikunta Chandra Nath, Bipin Chandra Nath and Lal Mohan Nath of Khatian No. 247. Tara Charan died leaving 2 sons Modan Mohan and Kali Charan. Gope Charan died leaving only son Chinta Haran and Modan Mohan died leaving only son Hari Nath. In the SA Khatian No. 155 name of Chinta Haran and Hari Nath were recorded. The owner of CS Khatian No. 147 Baikunta Chandra Nath died leaving 2 sons Baloram Nath and Kanai Nath. CS tenant Bipin Chandra Nath died leaving 2 sons Ballav Chandra Nath and Provash Chandra Nath. CS tenant Lal Mohan Nath died leaving 4 sons Haripada Nath, Shyam Sundar Nath, Surya Kumar Nath and Shisir Kumar Nath and their names were recorded in SA Khatian No. 181. The suit land of SA Khatian No. 155 along with other lands amicably got by Chinta Haran only son of Gope Mohan Nath and he sold his interest to the plaintiff on 26-4-1980. Suit land of SA Khatian No. 181 amicably got by Pravath Chandra Nath, the son of Bipin Chandra Nath and he sold his interest to the plaintiff on 17-7-1973 and accordingly, possession was handed over to the plaintiff. Plaintiff by filing Miscellaneous Case No. 483 of 1981 mutated her name and has been possessing the suit land on payment of rent to the government. At this stage the defendant No. 2 issued notice vide Memo No. 493 dated 11-7-1987 upon the plaintiff informing that the suit land is vested and non resident property. The plaintiff has filed the suit challenging the aforesaid Memo No. 493 dated 11-7-1987.

3. The defendant No. 1 contested the suit by filing written statement denying the material allegations made in the plaint and stated, inter alia, that the original and real owner of the suit land, the SA recorded tenant left this country in 1965 for India leaving this property. The property, thereafter, has been enlisted as vested and non resident property and the same is maintained by the defendant No. 2. Chinta Haran and Provath Chandra were not the citizens of this country and their names were not enlisted in the voter list rather they were the citizens of India. Husband of the plaintiff tried to get lease of the suit property on behalf of his wife admitting that the suit property as vested and non resident property in 1982 by filing application to the then SDO Munshiganj, but the prayer was rejected as the plaintiff was not in possession. Thereafter, the authority has leased out the land in VP Case No. 121 of 1974 and the land is in possession of the lease holders. The suit property is vested and non resident property and is being maintained by the Government; hence, the suit is liable to be dismissed.

4. The plaintiff examined 5 witnesses and the defendant examined 3 witnesses to prove their respective case.

5. The learned Assistant Judge after examining the evidence and records dismissed the suit by his judgment and decree dated 26-11-1990 and on 1-12-1990 respectively passed in Title Suit No. 60 of 1988.

6. The plaintiff being dissatisfied with the aforesaid judgment and decree of the Senior Assistant Judge preferred appeal being Title Appeal No. 3 of 1981 before the District Judge, Munshiganj.

7. The appeal was transferred to the Sub-ordinate Judge, Second Court, (Joint District Judge) for disposal of the Appeal. The learned Subordinate Judge after hearing the parties and upon perusing the evidence on record affirmed the judgment and decree of the trial Court.

8. The plaintiff again being dissatisfied with the judgment and decree aforesaid passed by the Appellate Court preferred revisional application and obtained the present Rule as stated above.

9. Mr Subrata Chowdhury, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the plaintiff petitioner, has taken me through the judgments of both the courts and during the argument he has placed the evidence as well as the exhibits and submitted that the deed executed by Provath Chandra Nath in favour of the plaintiff was registered at District Registrar Office Bakharganj on 17-7-1973 under section 30(2) of the Registration Act which was done before the amendment of Registration Act in 1985 legally and validly. The learned Advocate further submitted that the deed executed by Chinta Haran Nath in favour of Sreemoti Indrani Nath, the plaintiff at Sadar Sub-Registrar Office at Dhaka under section 7(2) of the Registration Act and such fact has been specifically endorsed by a 'seal' at the reverse of the deed and such act being done by public authority has evidentiary value and to prove such authority of the Sub-Registrar Sadar, Dhaka needs not to produce any paper as deed itself is containing such 'seal' showing authority and the appellate Court has committed no error of law in coming to the finding "according to section 30(2) of Registration Act any registrar can register any document without regard to the situation in any part of Bangladesh of the property to which the property relates if he is satisfied that there is sufficient cause for doing so." Though the vested and non resident property authority did not challenge the validity of such document either in the written statement or in the evidence but the courts below committed error of law in coming to findings that the plaintiff failed to prove her right and title over the suit land which has not been done according to law which is an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. The learned Advocate further submitted that by an alleged application said to have been made by husband of the plaintiff seeking lease of the suit property, cannot render the title of the vendors invalid as the original owners were not parties to that proceeding and such findings of the courts below are not based on proper appreciation of the law and, as such, coming to the findings that the plaintiff could not prove her right and title over the suit land have committed error of law. The learned Advocate further submitted that the DW 1 categorically stated in his evidence that they could not trace the census list in order to prove the contention to the effect that the property was declared enemy property or vested and non-resident property.

10. "The DW 1 further, during cross-examination, stated

“নাশিশী ভুমি অর্পিত হিসাবে পরিগনিত করার সময় শরীকদেরকে নোটিশ দেওয়া হইয়াছিল কিনা, নালিশী ভুমি সম্পর্কিত vested হওয়া মর্মে কোন census list অত্র উপজেলায় পাওয়া যায় নাই। ১৯৬৫ সনে নালিশী ভূমি হওয়া vested মর্মে কোন কাগজ পত্র দাখিল করেন নাই।”

11. DW 2 stated, during cross-examination, “চিন্তা হরণকে আমি পাকিস্তান আমলে দেখেছি ৬৭-৬৮ ইং সালে শুনেছি যে জমি বাদী খরিদ করেছে”

12. The learned Advocate, referring to the evidence of the DWs, submitted that those evidence were not considered by both the courts and thereby, came to wrong findings and committed error of law. He submitted further that the courts below failed to consider the registered deed dated 17-7-1973 and 26-4-1980 on the basis of which the plaintiff filed Miscellaneous Case No. 483 of 1980-81 and got her name mutated and those mutations clearly proved that the properties are not vested and non resident property and, without considering such aspect of the case, decided the case on wrong view which is an error in the decision occasioning failure of 'justice.

13. The learned Advocate further submit-ted the notice dated 11-7-1987 issued by the defendant No. 2 on the face of the record is illegal, inasmuch as after 23-7-1974 any letter treating the property as vested and non resident property is illegal and without jurisdiction which has been consistently held by the apex Court of the country and, in view of such decision of the apex court of the country, the courts in not giving decree holding that the property is not vested and non resident property have committed error of law.

14. The learned Advocate further submit-ted that the learned Assistant Judge has made out a 3rd case coming to the findings in deciding the issue No. 6 to the effect:

“নাঃ সম্পত্তিতে বাদীর কোন ধরনের কোন স্বত্ব দখল নাই এবং নাঃ জমির কোন এস এ, রায়ত নাঃ জমি দাবী করিতে আদালতে আসেন নাই। ফলে নাঃ জমি সরকারের উপর অর্পিত সম্পত্তি সে ক্ষেত্রে বিবাদী সরকার পক্ষ এস এ টি এ্যাক্ট এর বিধান মতে ও নাঃ জমি খাসে নিতে পারেন। বিষয়টি বিবাদী পক্ষে গ্রহন করা হইল।”

The Appellate Court, affirming such findings, has committed error of law which is an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. In support of his contention, Mr Subrata Chowdhury has referred a number of decisions such as:

1. In the case of Dulichand Omraolal vs Bangladesh, through the Secretary, Ministry of Industries reported in 33 DLR (AD) 30, wherein their Lordships of the Appellate Division held:

"11. We now revert back to the consequence of the continuance of Ordinance (1 of 1969). As stated earlier under Laws Continuance Enforcement Order, 1971 all laws in force on March 25, 1971 continued in force in Bangladesh as was consistent with the creation of sovereign Bangladesh and this position in law gets full recognition under President's Order No. 29 of 1972, Bangladesh (Vesting of Property and Assets) Order, 1972, and President's Order No. 48 of 1972 Bangladesh (Adaptation of Existing Bangladesh Laws) Order, 1972. President's Order No. 29 of 1972 vests all properties in the Government of Bangladesh which were vested in or managed by any Board constituted by or under any law or in the former Government of East Pakistan or Pakistan, President's Order No. 48 of 1972 provided for the adaptation of laws which were continued to rend amongst others Central Government or Government of East Pakistan on the Provincial Government or the Government of East Pakistan to refer to the People's Republic of Bangladesh. Then came Ordinance IV of 1974 the Enemy Property (Continuance of Emergency Provisions) (Repeal) Ordinance, 1974 which repealed the Enemy Property (Continuance of Emergency Provisions) Ordinance 1 of 1969 and provided, inter alia, that all enemy property vested in the Custodian of Enemy Property appointed under the provisions of the Defence of Pakistan. Rules continued in force by the said Ordinance shall vest in the Government, meaning Government of Bangladesh. There was another Ordinance No. V of 1974. The Vested and Non Resident Property (Administration) Ordinance 1974, which provided for the management and control of the vested and non-resident properties in the manner set out in the Ordinance. These Ordinances were replaced by Act XLV of 1974, Enemy Property (Continuance of Emergency Provisions) (Repeal) Act, 1974, and Act No. XLVI of 1974 the Vested and Non-Resident Property (Administration) Act, 1974. There had been two subsequent enactments, namely Ordinance XCII of 1976, the Vested and Non-Resident Property (Administration ) Repeal) Ordinance 1976 which repealed the Vested and Non-Resident Property (Administration) Act, 1974 followed by Ordinance XCIII of 1976 the Enemy Property (Continuance of Emergency Provision) (Repeal) (Amendment) Ordinance, 1976, which has amended section (3) of Act XLV of 1974 by providing that the properties which had vested in the Government, the right of administration, control, management and disposal of by transfer or otherwise be conferred on the Government or of such officer or authority as the Government may direct. This brings us to the up to date position of the enemy property laws which started with the Promulgation of Emergency and the Defence of Pakistan Ordinance and Rules made thereunder in 1965. We have already indicated that the continuance as a vested enemy property and there is no question of the vesting of the property by provisions other than contained in Rules 181 and 182. The effect of Provisions of Act XLV of 1974 as amended by Ordinance XCII and XCIII of 1976, is that the vesting of the property as enemy property by virtue of Defence of Pakistan Rules in the Custodian or Additional Custodian or the Board continued as vested property in the Government of Bangladesh. The vesting occurred by operation of aforesaid Defence of Pakistan Rules in those authorities and those vested properties as enemy properties as past and closed transaction continued to be so in the Government of Bangladesh and the Government acquired by the aforesaid laws all the right of management, control and disposal of the property by transfer or otherwise. Upon a true construction of the laws aforesaid, we get, that all rights in such property vest in the Government of Bangladesh and the title of the owner of the property remains subject to the overriding power of the Government or, in other words, the title of the owner remains eclipsed or suspended as long as property remains vested in the Government. The consequence is that the Government has all the power of management and disposal of those properties and also the power to release those properties. We, therefore, on facts, find that at first the Appellant firm on 20-9-1965 was declared as enemy property firm under Rule 181, and on 27-10-65 its properties were vested in the Additional Custodian under Rule 182 of the Defence of Pakistan Rules, were made during the currency of Emergency and so we find no error in the decision of the High Court that the firm did come within the definition of 'enemy firm' and so its assets were validity vested in the Additional Custodian as enemy property as vested enemy property, it continued by the successive legislations to remain so first, as enemy property and thereafter as vested property

2. 50 DLR (AD) 70. In the case of Government of Bangladesh vs Paresh Chandra Gharami reported in 50 DLR (AD) 70, wherein their Lordships observed:

"The trial Court dismissed the suit holding, inter alia, that the plaintiffs could not prove the basis of taking pattan of the suit land by their mother, Parbati Bala Gharami and that the defendant also could not prove the legal foundation of enlisting in the alleged census report the property as vested property (Exhibit-Ka). The trial Court however, found the plaintiffs possession in the suit land. The lower appellate Court set aside the decree of the trial Court and decreed the suit holding, inter alia, that the plaintiff-respondents, on the basis of Exhibit 1(Ka) and 1(Kha) namely, the judgment and decree of Title Suit No. 402 of 1958 and the compromise petition dated 23-8-59 respectively, proved their title to the suit land and that by Exhibit 2 series, 21 dakhilas, the certified copy of the khatians, opened in their mother's name on the basis of the decree of the aforesaid title suit and Exhibit 3 series Choukidari Tax receipts and the oral evidence proved their possession in title suit land and that the defendant could not prove the foundation of making the suit property as vested property. The High Court Division refused to interfere with these findings of fact in revision.

3. 56 DLR (AD) 73. In the case of Aroti Rani Paul vs Sudarshan Kumar Paul reported in 56 DLR (AD) 73, wherein their Lordships held:

"14. We have perused the judgments of the Courts below as well as the impugned judgment of the High Court Division. It appears that both the Courts below having considered the oral and documentary evidence, concurrently held that the transfer by registered deeds of 1975 vide Exhibits 5 and 6 as made by father and uncle, living in a joint undivided Hindu family under the Dayabhag School of Law, is valid. Since the father and uncle being in Bangladesh in the year 1975, transferred the suit property by the aforesaid deeds of gift, cannot be declared an enemy property in view of the aforesaid decision as referred to above in 46 DLR 136 and we accepted the argument of Mr Bhuiyan that since the law of enemy property itself died with the repeal of Ordinance No. 1 of 1969 on 23-3-1974 no further Vested Property case can be started thereafter on the basis of the law which is already dead."

15. Mr ABM Mahbub Suman, the learned Assistant Attorney-General appearing on behalf of the defendant-opposite party Nos.1 and 2, in refuting the submissions of the learned Advocate for the petitioner, has submitted that the facts of the case have been resolved by the courts below having considered the materials on record and, in such view of the matter, the judgments do not warrant any interference by this hon'ble court in revision. He submitted further that the trial Court found correctly and legally that the registration of the documents were not made having regard to the provision of the Registration Act and as such, the deeds cannot be treated as valid deeds and the plaintiff acquired no right, title, interest and possession having purchased the land from Chinta Haran and Provath and the appellate Court affirmed those findings having regard to Order XLI, rule 31 of the Code of Civil Procedure and in affirming the judgment and decree of the trial Court, the Appellate Court has committed no error of law which calls for no interference in revision by this Hon'ble Court.

16. On perusal of the judgment of the trial Court, it appears, amongst others, the trial Court held that the suit is not maintainable. The trial Court further held that the registration of the deeds having been registered in different places beyond the jurisdiction of the Sub-Registrar Sirajdikhan, those deeds were not validly done and on the basis of those documents the plaintiff acquired no right, title, interest and possession in the suit land. The trial Court also held, in deciding issue No.6, that the government may resume the property under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act as both plaintiff and the defendant failed to prove the respective contention. The appellate Court, on the other hand, affirmed the judgment of the trial Court and came to the findings:

"The suit property situated tinder the jurisdiction of Sub-Registrar Sirajdikhan. But the plaintiff registered Kabala deed No.6278 dated 19-7-1973 from Bakerganj District Registrar. To support the cause of registration in Bakerganj plaintiff has filed voter list Exhibit-4 to show that the transferor was the inhabitant and voter of Mehendigonj Thana of Bakerganj District. I think only the voter list is not sufficient ground to get the protection of section 30(2) of the Registration Act. Kabala deed No. 15340 dated 26-4-80 was registered in Dhaka under section 7(2) of the Registration Act. But the plaintiff did not file any paper to support the version of section 7(2) to prove the amalgamation of Sirajdikhan Sub-Registrar Office with the district of Dhaka. So, it can easily be presumed that plaintiff has registered both the Kabalas by defeating the law of registration and to grab the suit land."

<u>17. On perusal of the judgments of both the courts, it appears that the courts below failed to notice the evidence of DW 1 that the DW 1 could not produce the census list which is the legal foundation for treating the suit property as enemy property or vested and non-resident property. It further appears that the courts below on consideration of the application of the husband of the plaintiff held that the plaintiff's husband as well as the plaintiff admitted the property to be the vested and non resident property but such findings of the Court below are not based on law, inasmuch as by mere admission of a third party as to vested property other than the real owner, such findings have got no basis, inasmuch as the admission of a third party cannot thus disentitle a real owner to claim his title over his own land and such findings do not appeal to any reasons, as such, findings are not based in law. It appears further that the deed by Private that was executed on 17-7-1973 in favour of the plaintiff was registered in Bakerganj, District Registrar Office as contemplated under section 30(2) of the Registration Act before the amendment of Registration Act in 1985 which, in my opinion, had been done legally. The deed executed by Chinta Haran was registered at Sadar Sub-Registrar Office at Dhaka under section 7(2) of the Registration Act and such authority is evident from the reverse of the deed. The registration of the deed made under such authority by a public officer has got evidentiary value. So, the registration of his deed appears to have been done legally. The evidence of DW 1 has clearly indicated that the government failed to prove the legal foundation for enlisting the suit property as enemy property producing the census list and if the foundation goes, in that case, the version of the plaintiff that she purchased the land by 2 registered deeds get support of her interest in the suit property. Over all, on the evaluation of the evidence along with the judgments of both the courts, it has been revealed that the Courts below committed error of law in holding that the plaintiff could not prove her right, title and possession in the suit land which is an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. It appears further that the plaintiff only sought declaration to the effect that the notice issued by the defendant No.2 dated 11-7-1987 is illegal, void and not binding upon the plaintiff but the courts below, as it appears from the record, made endeavour to settle the title of the plaintiff which apparently was a  approach to the pleadings of the parties. It further reveals that the courts below have made out a third case holding that the Government may resume the land under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act as the plaintiff and the defendant failed to prove their respective case but such views cannot be approved rather should be deprecated.</u>

18. In view of my discussions made above, I find substance in the submissions of the learned Advocate for the petitioner and, as such, the Rule has merit.

19. In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs. The judgment and decree dated 13-7-1994 passed by Sub-ordinate Judge, Munshiganj in Tile Appeal No.3 of 1991 affirming the judgment and decree dated 26-11-1990 and 1-12-1990 respectively passed by the Senior Assistant Judge, Munshiganj in Title Suit No.60 of 1988 are set aside. The suit is decreed as in terms of the prayer 'Ka' and thereby, declared the memo No.493 dated 11-7-1987 issued by defendant No.2 in VP Case No.121 of 1974 (Sirajdikhan) is illegal, void and not binding upon the plaintiff.

Send down the lower courts records immediately.

End.

full_judgment:
This Rule under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure was issued at the instance of plaintiffs as petitioners, directing the defendant opposite parties to show cause why the judgment and decree dated 14-7-1992 passed by the Subordinate Judge, Patuakhali in Title Appeal No. 144 of 1991 reversing those dated 24-9-1991 passed by the Assistant Judge, Galachipa, Patuakhali in Title Suit No. 81 of 1985 should not be set aside and/or pass such other or further order or orders as to this court may seem fit and proper.

2. Short fact, necessary for the purpose of this Rule, is that the petitioners as plaintiffs instituted Title Suit No. 81 of 1985 before the Assistant Judge, Galachipa, Patuakhali impleading the opposite parties as defendants seeking a decree for declaration of their title in the suit land stating, inter alia, that the land appertaining to CS Khatian Nos. 17, 217, 218, of Mouja Chhailabunia of Police-Station-Galachipa originally belonged to Araj Ali to the extent of one-third share, who having been in possession and enjoyment thereof died leaving behind one son the plaintiffs No.1 and two daughters Aziful Bibi, Karful Bibi, and a wife Meherjan as his heirs; Karful Bibi died unmarried leaving behind her mother Meherjan, brother the plaintiff No.1 and a sister Aziful Bibi the plaintiff No. 2. Thereafter, Meherjan died leaving behind the plaintiff Nos.1 and 2 as her sole heirs; it is also, stated by the plaintiffs that during SA operation plaintiffs' share was wrongly recorded as 2 annas 13 gandas I Kara and I Karanti. Though as a matter of fact the remaining 2 annas 13 gondas I Kara I Karanti share was wrongly recorded in favour of some of the defendants as also in favour of the predecessors of some others, who have no right, title, interest or possession therein; it was further stated in the plaint that on 13-5-1985 when the defendants attempted to invade the right of the plaintiffs over the suit land on the basis of such erroneous record of right the plaintiffs brought the suit claiming their title in the suit land which has been in their possession, as stated above.

3. The defendant No. 4 entered appearance upon filing written statement denying the material allegations made in the plaint contending, inter alia, that the plaintiffs have no right, title, interest or possession in the suit land appertaining to CS Khatian Nos.17, 217, 218 and 219, rather one Alef Chowkider was the exclusive owner in possession of the said land; said Alef Chowkider married Mayajan the mother of one Sharap Ali who was the grandfather of defendant No. 4 while Araj Ali is the son of Mohammed Jan who was the former husband of Maynajan. It was further alleged in the written statement that one-third share was collusively recorded in favour of the predecessor of the plaintiffs during CS operation which was not correct; Alef Chowkikder gifted away some land to the extent of 1.52 acres in favour of Sharaf Ali by a deed of gift dated 14 Falgoon 1326 BS and had handed over possession; it was also stated in the written statement that Araj Ali also executed a nadabinama in respect of the said land in favour of Sworup Ali on 28 Chaitra, 1344 BS. Subsequently, the SA record was correctly prepared in his favour, the plaintiffs have no right, title, interest or possession in the suit land hence the suit was liable to be dismissed.

4. It was also stated in the written statement that a suit being Title Suit No.106 of 1968 was instituted by the plaintiffs in respect of selfsame land against the defendants but it was withdrawn on 27-3-1969 with a permission to sue afresh, as such, the instant suit is also barred by limitation.

5. Eventually, the suit was taken up for hearing by the Assistant Judge where the plaintiffs examined 3 witnesses while the defendants examined 4 witnesses on their behalf and upon conclusion of the trial the Assistant Judge decreed the suit by his Judgment and decree dated 24-9-91 in Title Suit No.81 of 1985.

6. As against the aforesaid judgment and decree dated 24-9-1991 passed by the trial Court the defendant No.4 as appellant preferred Title Appeal No.144 of 1991 before the District Judge, Patuakhali which on transfer was heard by the Subordinate Judge, Patuakhali who having heard the appeal allowed the same by his judgment and decree dated 14-7-1992, reversing the decree of the trial Court.

7. As against the aforesaid judgment and decree of reversal dated 14-7-1992 passed in Title Appeal No.144 of 1991, the plaintiffs as petitioners obtained the instant Rule.

8. Mr Golam Arshed, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner, submits that the impugned judgment and decree as passed by the appellate Court below is not a proper judgment of reversal, in that it is violative of the mandatory provision of Order XLI, rule 31 of the Code of Civil Procedure. In elaborating his submission, the learned Advocate submits further that the trial Court upon consideration of the evidence and materials on record arrived at a positive finding to the effect that the plaintiffs have been able to establish their right, title and possession in the suit land but the appellate Court reversed the decision of the trial Court without adverting to the aforesaid finding arrived at by the trial Court rather affirmed these findings in his judgment. The learned Advocate for the petitioner submits further that the appellate Court below allowed the appeal upon reversing the decision of the trial Court merely on the point of limitation erroneously holding that the suit is barred by limitation. In substantiating his submission the learned Advocate referred to the finding of the appellate Court below to the effect that the previous suit namely, Title Suit No.106 of 1968 was withdrawn on 27-3-1969 with a permission to sue afresh on the same cause of action with a condition to pay Rupees 50 to the credit of contesting defendant, but the instant suit being Title Suit No. 21 of 1985 had been instituted on 3-8-1985 long after an interval of about 16 (sixteen) years, as such, the suit was, according to the Appellate Court, barred by limitation. Mr Golam Arshed, the learned Advocate, submits that the instant suit being Title Suit No. 81 of 1985 is neither filed on the same cause of action nor the relief claimed in the earlier suit is the same as that of the present one. According to the learned Advocate, the previous suit was filed on a different cause of action accrued at that relevant time while the present suit has been filed with the cause of action accrued on 13-5-1985 on which date the defendants threatened to invade the right of the plaintiffs over the suit land, the learned Advocate submits further that in the previous suit the relief claimed was that of correction of record of right and declaration of title while in the present suit the plaintiffs have simply prayed for declaration of their title in the suit land and no prayer for correction of record of right has been made. Therefore, the learned Advocate submits that the subject matter in the previous suit with that of the present suit is not the same and in substantiating his submission the learned Advocate refers to the decision of Bhagavan Das Mohesri vs Prosannan Dev Raiket and others reported in AIR 1934 Calcutta 433, wherein a Division Bench of Calcutta High Court relying on AIR 1917 Born 10 and 431 C 752 followed the decision to the effect:

"The question is whether the previous suit was a suit for the same "subject-matter" within the meaning of Order XXIII, rule 1. We are of opinion that "Subject-matter" means, to use the word of 1.I, R.I, the series of acts or transactions alleged to exist giving rise to the relief claimed. Obviously, the first series of acts or transactions which formed the basis of the first suit was incomplete, or the plaintiff would have been able to prosecute his suit to decree. It was incomplete because there was no notice to quit. The second series of acts or transactions is complete because the notice to quit has been given, and therefore, the two suits are not in respect of the same "subject-matter."

9. In this case no one has appeared on behalf of the opposite parties to oppose the Rule despite due service of notice upon them. Under such circumstances I have myself gone through the materials on record including the impugned judgments passed by the Courts below as also heard by the learned Advocate for the petitioner.

<u>10. Upon consideration of the aforesaid materials and submission of the learned Advocate for the petitioner, particularly when he relied upon the decision given by a Division Bench of Calcutta High Court as referred to above, wherefrom I find that the said decision has got a direct bearing in the present case. More particularly, when the earlier suit, being Title Suit No. 106 of 1968, was a suit for correction of record of right disclosing a particular cause of action arose in the year 1968, while the present suit being Title Suit No. 81 of 1985 was instituted seeking a decree for simple declaration of title on the basis of a cause of action which arose on 13-5-1985 when a threat of invasion of the right of the plaintiffs was demonstrated by the defendants then only the plaintiffs took recourse to institution of the present suit. This Court being in respectful agreement with the principle of law enunciated in the case referred to above, also finds that the expression subject matter as used in Order XXIII rule I means a series of acts or transactions alleged to exist giving rise to the relief claimed. As such, the first series of facts or transactions, which formed the basis of the first suit being Title Suit No.106 of 1968 was based on erroneous record of right, in the SA Khatian and the suit was brought from the date of knowledge with respect to such wrong record of right but in the instant suit namely, Title Suit No. 81 of 1985, the date of threatened invasion over the right of the plaintiffs on 13-5-1985 was the cause of action and not the erroneous record of right, besides the relief claimed in that suit cannot be said to be one and the same. Therefore, in my opinion, the previous suit was instituted with a different subject matter than that of the present suit and that the relief claimed in that suit is not the same as in the present case besides, the cause of action in that suit is not the same as in the present one. Therefore, institution of the previous suit cannot have any bearing in instituting the present suit and in that view of the matter, the institution of the previous suit cannot be a ground for treating the present suit as one barred by limitation under Article 122 of the Limitation Act.</u>

<u>11. It has also been noticed that the appellate Court did not find any reason to differ with the trial Court in respect of title and possession of the plaintiffs in the suit land, rather the finding of the trial Court in that respect has been concurrently affirmed by the appellate Court yet dismissed the suit merely on the ground of limitation which, in m opinion, has been arrived at on misconception of the provision of law as embodied in both Article 122 of the Limitation Act as also of the expression used in Order XXIII rule I of the Code of Civil Procedure. In view of the discussions made above, the impugned judgment and decree of reversal call for interference by this court.</u>

12. In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs and the impugned judgment and decree of reversal dated 14-7-1992 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, now joint District Judge in Title Appeal No.144 of 1991 is hereby set aside and the judgment and decree dated 24-9-1991 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Galachiipa in Title Suit No. 81 of Title Suit No.81 of 1985 is hereby upheld.

Send down a copy of this judgment along with the lower Court's record to the trial Court at once.

End.

full_judgment:
This revision application is directed against the judgment and decree dated 24-4-1994 passed by the Additional District Judge, Bagerhat in Title Appeal No. 212 of 1984 allowing the appeal and reversing those dated 18-5-1983 passed by the Subordinate Judge, Bagerhat in Title suit No. 236 of 1981 dismissing the suit.

2. The petitioners as plaintiffs filed the suit for declaration of title to the suit land on the averments, inter alia, that 10.23 acres of land out of the land recorded in CS Khatian No. 140 and 4.31 acres of land recorded in CS Khatian No. 280 originally belonged to 3 full brothers, namely Judu Nath Mondal, Paban Mondal and Gogon Mondal in equal share. Paban Mondal died leaving behind a son, Banomali, Judu Nath Mondal died leaving behind a widow Totamoni, daughter named, Ayna Moni and defendants No. 4-6 daughters sons born out of the womb of Aynamoni. The land of CS Khatian No. 140 was recorded in the name of Tota Moni, Gagon Mondal and Banamali Mondal in equal share and SA Khatian No. 329 was also prepared in their names, 4.31 acres of land recorded in CS Khatian No. 280 was acquired with the income of the joint family in the name of Judu Nath Mondal and it was recorded as such in his name in the aforesaid CS Khatian No. 280. The said land was recorded in the name of Totamoni, Gagon Mondal and Banomali in equal share in SA Khatian 116. Defendants No. 4-6 and Totamoni sold 3.35 acres of land from CS Khatian No. 140 and 1.36 acres of land from CS Khatian No. 280, that is, in total 4.71 acres of land to Gagon Mondal by a kabala dated 29-4-1963 and delivered possession thereof to him. The plaintiffs have been possessing the aforesaid land all through. The plaintiffs could not withdraw the original kabala from the concerned sub-registrar's office as they lost the ticket. Defendants No. 4-6 created 3 collusive kabalas in favour of defendant Nos. 1-3 and having been armed with the aforesaid kabalas defendant Nos. 1-3 threatened the plaintiffs with dispossession from the suit land on 20-12-1976 and hence the suit.

3. Opposite party Nos. 1-3 as defendant No. 1-3 contested the suit by filing a joint written statement contending, inter alia, that the land of CS khatian No. 280 was the self acquired property of Judu Nath Mondal. The kabala dated 29-4-1963 was never acted upon. Defendant Nos. 4-6 sold the suit land along with other lands to defendant Nos. 1-3 by 3 separate kabalas dated 28-10-1976 and delivered possession thereof to them and they are in possession of the suit land. The plaintiffs having no right, title and interest to the suit land as well as possession therein were not entitled to get any relief and the suit was liable to be dismissed.

<u>4. On conclusion of the nearing of the suit, the learned Subordinate Judge by his judgment and decree dated 18-5-1998 decreed the suit on the finding, inter alia, that the suit was not barred by limitation, the suit was maintainable in its present form and was not hit by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, that the plaintiff have title to and possession in suit land. Being aggrieved by the said judgment and decree of the trial Court the contesting defendants preferred Title Appeal No. 212 of 1984 before the District Judge, Bagerhat. The appeal was eventually heard by the learned Additional District Judge, Bagerhat who by the impugned judgment and decree allowed the appeal and dismissed the suit.</u>

5. Mr SS Sarker, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners, submits that the trial Court on consideration of the evidence on record, both oral and documentary, particularly the evidence of PWs 1, 4, 5 and DW 2, the khatians, exhibits 1(a) 1(b) and the rent receipts, ext 2 series came to the definite finding that after purchase of the suit land by kabala dated 29-4-1963 the plaintiffs went into the possession of the suit land and have been in possession thereof, but the appellate Court being the final court of fact did not consider the evidence on record in deciding the question of possession of the suit land and as to whether the kabala was acted upon. He further submits that, in fact, the appellate Court set aside the Judgment and decree of the trial Court only dealing with the question of passing of consideration in respect of the kabala in question, dated 29-4-1963 but in dealing with the said question it failed to consider that in the written statement filed by the contesting defendants no such case was made out, as such, the evidence led to that effect by the DWs being beyond the pleading was not admissible in evidence, the appellate Court erroneously relief upon the said part of the evidence in not finding title of the plaintiff to the suit land on the basis of their purchase dated 29-4-1963 and thereby committed error of law in dismissing the suit. Mr Barker further submits that in order to meet the finding of the appellate Court as to the maintainability of the suit in not making any prayer for consequential relief the plaintiff petitioners have filed an application under Order VI, rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure for amendment of the plaint praying for confirmation of joint possession in the suitland along with the prayer for declaration of title and there being overwhelming evidence on record that the plaintiffs are in possession of the suit land the prayer for amendment of the plaint may be allowed.

6. A counter-affidavit has been filed on behalf of opposite party Nos. 1-3 opposing the prayer for amendment. In the counter-affidavit it has been stated that the application for amendment has been filed after about 27 years from the date of filing of the suit with malafide motive just to fill up the lacuna of the plaintiff's case and, as such, the same cannot be allowed. It has further been stated that if the prayer for amendment is allowed it would take away the valuable right accrued to the defendants after the suit was dismissed by the appellate Court and thus the defendants shall be seriously prejudiced.

7. The amendment sought for is as under:

“১ ৷ আরজির চার নম্বর দফার নীচে নিম্নলিখিত কথাগুলি লিখিতে হইবে যাহা চার দফার অংশ হিসেবে বিবেচিত হইবে ৷ সি,এস, ১৪০ খতিয়ানে নালিশী ৮৬৪ দাগে ৪.৩৩ একর, ৮৬৩ দাগে ৩.৯৩ একর, ২৮৩ দাগে ০.৩৫ একর এবং ২৮৫ দাগে ০.১ ১ একর একুনে ৭.৯২ একর ভূমির মধ্যে পশ্চিম পার্শ্ব দিয়া ৩.৩৫ একর ভূমিতে তোতামনি স্বামীর ওয়ারীশ সূত্রে স্বত্ব খান ও দখলীকার ছিলেন বটে ৷ এবং সি,এসম ২৮০ নম্বর খতিয়ানের নালিশী ৩৭ দাগে ০.২১ একর সম্পূর্ণ, ৩৮ দাগে ০.২২ একর সম্পূর্ণ, ৪০ দাগে ৩.৬৯ একর মধ্যে পূর্বপার্শ্ব হইতে ০.৯৩ একর একুনে ১.৩৬ একর জমিতে পূর্বোক্ত তোতামনি স্বত্ববর্তী ও দখলকারী থাকা কালে তোতামনি ও ৪-৬নং বিবাদী উপযুক্ত মূল্য গ্রহণে এই বাদীগণের পূর্ববর্তী গগনমন্ডল বরাবরে বিক্রয় করেন ও তাহাকে দখল প্রতিষ্ঠিত করেন ৷ উক্ত ৮৬৪, ৮৬৩, ২৮৩, ২৮৫ ও ৪০ দাগের অবশিষ্ট জমিতে অর্থাৎ ৭.৩৩ শতক জমিতে এই বাদীগণ ও অপর শরীক বনোমালী মন্ডলের ওয়ারিশ ৭-১০ নং বিবাদীগন এজমালিতে দখলকার ছিলেন ও আছেন অর্থাৎ উক্ত দাগ গুলিতে বর্তমান এই বাদীগণ ও ৭-১০ নং বিবাদীগণ নালিশী জমিতে এজমালিতে দখলিকার ছিলেন ও আছেন। এবং নালিশী জমি শুধুমাত্র যদু নাথের অংশের জমি হইতেছে এবং উহার অত্র মামলার নালিশী জমি হইতেছে।

২ ৷ আরজির ৯ নম্বর দফার ক নম্বর প্রার্থনাটি কাটা যাইবে, তদস্থলে নিম্নলিখিত প্রার্থনাটি যোগ করিতে হইবে ৷

“আরজি বর্ণিত মতে নালিশী জমিতে বাদীগেণর অনুকূলে স্বত্ব সাব্যস্ত পূর্বক ৭-১০ নং বিবাদীগণের সহিত এজমালিক দখল কায়েমের ডিক্রি হয়।

৩ ৷ আরজির ৮নং দফার “স্বত্ব প্রচার বাবদ নির্দিষ্ট কোর্ট ফি ২০ (কুড়ি) টাকা প্রদান করা গেল" কথাগুলি কাটা যাইবে তদস্থলে “এ্যাডভেলোরেম কোর্ট ফি প্রদান করা হইল ।”

<u>8. I have considered the plaint. It appears to me that amendment of the plaint sought for as quoted above is quite in conformity with the plaint case and if the same is allowed that would in no way change the nature and character of the suit and the plaint. From the judgments of the courts below it appears that the trial Court gave the finding of possession of the suitland in favour of the plaintiffs, but the appellate Court did not reverse the said finding of the trial Court with reference to the evidence on record. The trial Court gave clear finding that though DW 1 Aroz Ali claimed possession of the suit land through their bargadars, namely, Shamsu and Keramat, yet none of the said persons was examined in order to prove their possession in the suit land, Mr Ramjan Ali Khan tried to argue that non examination of the bargadars cannot be a ground to disbelieve other DWs in deciding the factum of possession of the suitland. The submission of Mr Khan cannot be accepted for the simple reason that DW 1 deposed that they possess the suit land through bargadars, therefore, it was incumbent upon them to examine the bargadars. And for non examination of the bargadars an adverse presumption can very much be drawn against the defendants under section 114(g) of the Evidence Act.</u>

9. I have also gone through the evidence on record. I find that the finding of possession of the trial Court is based on evidence on record, Since the plaintiffs are found in possession of the suit land, I do not see any bar to allow the prayer for joint possession with defendant Nos. 7-10 along with declaration of title. I am also of the view that if the plaintiffs prayer for amendment of the plaint is not allowed they will be deprived of their legitimate right of enjoyment of their valuable properties Mr AS Md Ramzan Khan, the learned Advocate appearing for the defendants, vehemently opposes the prayer for amendment of the plaint on the ground that the application has been filed after long 27 years. In view of the settled proposition of law that amendment of the pleading can be allowed at any stage of the proceedings provided that the amendment if allowed would neither change the nature and character of the suit nor the plaint and is necessary to decide the questions involved in the suit, I do not find any substance in the submission or Mr Khan, Therefore, I allow the prayer for amendment of the plaint. Let the amendment be incorporated in the plaint. The office is directed to do the needful.

<u>10. From the judgment of the appellate Court it appears that it dismissed the suit on 3(three) grounds, first one being that the suit was not maintainable as no consequential relief was prayed for and second one being that the suit land was vague. In view of the amendment of the plaint the said two grounds have lost their factual and legal force. The third ground is that the plaintiffs did not acquire any title to the suit land by virtue of their purchase by kabala dated 29-4-1963 as consideration for the kabala in question did not pass. I have gone through the written statement filed by the contesting defendants but no such case was made out in the written statement and, as such, the evidence led by the defendants in that respect was inadmissible in evidence. In this regard the provision of rule 7 of Order VI of the Code of Civil Procedure may be referred to which is as under:</u>

<u>"No pleading shall, except by way of amendment, raise any new ground of claim or contain any allegation of fact inconsistent with the previous pleadings of the same.</u>

<u>Besides, the finding of the trial Court as to the passing of consideration is based on evidence on record, being consistent with the finding of possession than the finding given by the appellate Court. Therefore, I find substance in the submission of Mr Sarker and consequently, the said ground of the appellate Court in dismissing the suit also does not stand.</u>

11. For the discussions made above, I hold that the appellate Court committed error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice in passing the impugned judgment and decree allowing the appeal and dismissing the suit.

In the result, this Rule is made absolute without any order as to cost. The impugned Judgment and decree is set aside. The Judgment and decree passed by the trial Court is restored with the modification that the suit be decree declaring plaintiffs' title to the suitland and confirming their joint possession there in with defendant Nos. 7-10. The plaintiffs are directed to pay the ad-valorem Court fees on the valuation of the suit within 2(two) months from the date of receipt of the Judgment passed by this Court, in default the Rule shall stand discharged and the suit dismissed.

End.
